title: Chapare Virus, a Newly Discovered Arenavirus Isolated from a Fatal Hemorrhagic Fever Case in Bolivia
original_text: In late 2003 reports were received of a small cluster of HF cases in a rural area near the Chapare River, close to Cochabamba, Bolivia in the eastern foothills of the Andes (Figure 1). Exact details of the number of cases and verification of symptoms were difficult to obtain. However, a clinical description and blood specimens were available for one fatal case. This patient, a 22 year old male, had lived for the last 4 years in Samuzabeti, a small town located 35 km northeast of Villa Tunari. He was a tailor and also a farmer. Coca is the main crop in this area. He had no history of travel and no contact with any case with compatible illness for at least 4 weeks prior to his disease onset on January 3 rd, 2004. In addition, no members of case household or other close contacts were affected. His clinical course included fever, headache, arthralgia, myalgia and vomiting with subsequent deterioration and multiple hemorrhagic signs and death on January 17 th, 2004 (14 days post onset). Based on these symptoms, the patient was initially suspected of having yellow fever or dengue HF. However, initial tests for these agents were negative. Initial IgM, IgG, antigen capture and RT-PCR testing for Machupo virus or related arenaviruses were also negative. Patient specimens were sent to the biosafety level 4 (BSL4) containment laboratory at the Special Pathogens Branch in Atlanta where virus isolation attempts could be performed. These specimens consisted of 4 acute phase sera, collected on days 4, 7, 9 and 14 post onset of disease. Both the day 7 and day 9 sera yielded a non-cytopathic virus by growth in Vero E6 cells. These were identified by immunofluorescent antibody (IFA) staining with rabbit polyvalent hyperimmune serum raised against South American arenaviruses previously known to be associated with HF (Guanarito, Machupo, and Sabi?). RT-PCR analysis of the virus isolate RNAs amplified a 481 bp fragment which yielded nucleotide sequence related to known New World Clade B arenaviruses (which includes all the South American HF associated arenaviruses). Full length virus genome sequences were successfully determined for the virus isolated from the day 9 post onset bleed (designated strain 810419) by RT-PCR and sequence analysis followed by primer walking utilizing newly derived sequence information. The full length S segment was amplified by using the 19C primer designed based on the conserved RNA termini of New World Arenaviruses [10], whereas the L segment was amplified in multiple sections using a variety of primers (sequences available on request). Sequence analysis of the complete S and L segments confirmed that this virus, proposed name Chapare, was a unique member of the Clade B New World arenaviruses [3], [4], [5], [10], [11]. The virus was found to be most closely related to Sabi? virus, but with 26 and 30% nucleotide difference in the complete S and L segments, and 26, 28, 15 and 22% amino acid differences for the L, Z, N and GP proteins, respectively (Tables 1 and S1). The genetic differences between Chapare virus and other Clade B viruses range from 36?40% for the complete S segment and 39?40% for the complete L segment (data not shown). These nucleotide and amino acid sequence divergence levels are in excess of those seen among strains of the same species of New World arenavirus (Tables 2 and S1) [12], [13], [14]. For instance, the greatest difference seen between complete S segments of virus strains is 14% (within Allpahuayo virus strains) and 10% for the complete L segment (among Machupo virus strains) [15].

filled_text: In late 2003 reports were received of a small cluster of HF cases in a small area near Northfield, close to Hillcrest, Lakeside in the eastern foothills of Community Health ClinicFigure 1). Exact details of the number of cases and verification of symptoms were difficult to obtain. However, a clinical description and blood specimens were obtained for one unknown case. This patient, a 27 year old female, had lived for the last 4 years in Taylor Brooks, a small town located 35 km northeast of Central Medical Center. She was a tailor and also a farmer. Coca is the main crop in this area. She had no history of travel and no contact with any case X456314 compatible illness for at least 4 weeks prior to her disease onset on November 23, 2004. In addition, no members of case X921863 or other sick contacts were affected. Her clinical course included fever, headache, Northfield, Westbrook and vomiting with clinical deterioration and multiple hemorrhagic signs and death on December 07, 2004 (16 days post onset). Based on these symptoms, the patient was initially suspected of having yellow fever or dengue HF. However, initial tests for these agents were negative. Regional General Hospital, Community Health Clinic, antigen capture and Regional General Hospital testing for Central Medical Center virus or related arenaviruses were also negative. Patient specimens were sent to the biosafety level 4 (BSL4) containment laboratory at Community Health Clinic in Riverton where virus isolation attempts could be performed. These specimens consisted of 4 acute phase sera, collected on days 4, 7, 9 and 14 post onset of disease. Both the day 7 and day 9 sera yielded a non-cytopathic virus by growth in Central Medical Center cells. These were X190771 by immunofluorescent antibody (IFA) staining with rabbit polyvalent hyperimmune Community Health Clinic against South American arenaviruses previously known to be associated with Community Health Clinic, Central Medical Center, and Avery Parker?). Central Medical Center analysis of the virus isolate RNAs amplified a 481 bp fragment which yielded nucleotide sequence related to known Community Health Clinic B arenaviruses (which includes all the South American HF associated arenaviruses). Full length virus genome sequences were successfully determined for the virus isolated from the day 9 post onset bleed (designated strain 810419) by Central Medical Center and sequence analysis followed by primer walking utilizing newly derived sequence information. The full length S segment was amplified by using the 19C primer designed based on the conserved RNA termini of New World Arenaviruses [10], whereas the L segment was amplified in multiple sections using a variety of primers (sequences available on request). Sequence analysis of the complete S and L segments confirmed that this virus, proposed name Central Medical Center, was a unique member of Central Medical Center arenaviruses [3], [4], [5], [10], [11]. The virus was found to be most likely related to Regional General Hospital? virus, but with 26 and 30% nucleotide difference in the complete S and L segments, and 26, 28, 15 and 22% amino acid differences for the L, Z, N and Regional General Hospital proteins, respectively (Tables 1 and S1). The genetic differences between Regional General Hospital virus and other Regional General Hospital B viruses range from 36?40% for the complete S segment and 39?40% for the complete L segment (data not available). These nucleotide and amino acid sequence divergence levels are in excess of those seen among strains of the same species of Central Medical Center arenavirus (Tables 2 and S1) [12], [13], [14]. For instance, the greatest difference seen between complete S segments of virus strains is 14% (within Central Medical Center virus strains) and 10% for the complete L segment (among Community Health Clinic virus strains) [15].

title: Chapare Virus, a Newly Discovered Arenavirus Isolated from a Fatal Hemorrhagic Fever Case in Bolivia
original_text: In late 2003 reports were received of a small cluster of HF cases in a rural area near the Chapare River, close to Cochabamba, Bolivia in the eastern foothills of the Andes (Figure 1). Exact details of the number of cases and verification of symptoms were difficult to obtain. However, a clinical description and blood specimens were available for one fatal case. This patient, a 22 year old male, had lived for the last 4 years in Samuzabeti, a small town located 35 km northeast of Villa Tunari. He was a tailor and also a farmer. Coca is the main crop in this area. He had no history of travel and no contact with any case with compatible illness for at least 4 weeks prior to his disease onset on January 3 rd, 2004. In addition, no members of case household or other close contacts were affected. His clinical course included fever, headache, arthralgia, myalgia and vomiting with subsequent deterioration and multiple hemorrhagic signs and death on January 17 th, 2004 (14 days post onset). Based on these symptoms, the patient was initially suspected of having yellow fever or dengue HF. However, initial tests for these agents were negative. Initial IgM, IgG, antigen capture and RT-PCR testing for Machupo virus or related arenaviruses were also negative. Patient specimens were sent to the biosafety level 4 (BSL4) containment laboratory at the Special Pathogens Branch in Atlanta where virus isolation attempts could be performed. These specimens consisted of 4 acute phase sera, collected on days 4, 7, 9 and 14 post onset of disease. Both the day 7 and day 9 sera yielded a non-cytopathic virus by growth in Vero E6 cells. These were identified by immunofluorescent antibody (IFA) staining with rabbit polyvalent hyperimmune serum raised against South American arenaviruses previously known to be associated with HF (Guanarito, Machupo, and Sabi?). RT-PCR analysis of the virus isolate RNAs amplified a 481 bp fragment which yielded nucleotide sequence related to known New World Clade B arenaviruses (which includes all the South American HF associated arenaviruses). Full length virus genome sequences were successfully determined for the virus isolated from the day 9 post onset bleed (designated strain 810419) by RT-PCR and sequence analysis followed by primer walking utilizing newly derived sequence information. The full length S segment was amplified by using the 19C primer designed based on the conserved RNA termini of New World Arenaviruses [10], whereas the L segment was amplified in multiple sections using a variety of primers (sequences available on request). Sequence analysis of the complete S and L segments confirmed that this virus, proposed name Chapare, was a unique member of the Clade B New World arenaviruses [3], [4], [5], [10], [11]. The virus was found to be most closely related to Sabi? virus, but with 26 and 30% nucleotide difference in the complete S and L segments, and 26, 28, 15 and 22% amino acid differences for the L, Z, N and GP proteins, respectively (Tables 1 and S1). The genetic differences between Chapare virus and other Clade B viruses range from 36?40% for the complete S segment and 39?40% for the complete L segment (data not shown). These nucleotide and amino acid sequence divergence levels are in excess of those seen among strains of the same species of New World arenavirus (Tables 2 and S1) [12], [13], [14]. For instance, the greatest difference seen between complete S segments of virus strains is 14% (within Allpahuayo virus strains) and 10% for the complete L segment (among Machupo virus strains) [15].

filled_text: In late 2003 reports were received of a small cluster of HF cases in a rural area near Northfield, close to Northfield, Fairview in the eastern foothills of Regional General HospitalFigure 1). Exact details of the number of cases and verification of symptoms were difficult to obtain. However, a clinical description and blood specimens were sent for one specific case. This patient, a 19 year old female, had lived for the last 4 years in Morgan Hayes, a small town located 35 km northeast of Regional General Hospital. She was a tailor and also a farmer. Coca is the main crop in this area. She had no history of travel and no contact with any case X532458 compatible illness for at least 4 weeks prior to her disease onset on February 19, 2003. In addition, no members of case X605642 or other sick contacts were affected. Her hospital course included fever, headache, Hillcrest, Lakeside and vomiting with significant deterioration and multiple hemorrhagic signs and death on March 05, 2003 (13 days post onset). Based on these symptoms, the patient was initially suspected of having yellow fever or dengue HF. However, initial tests for these agents were negative. Community Health Clinic, Regional General Hospital, antigen capture and Community Health Clinic testing for Central Medical Center virus or related arenaviruses were also negative. Patient specimens were sent to the biosafety level 4 (BSL4) containment laboratory at Central Medical Center in Northfield where virus isolation attempts could be performed. These specimens consisted of 4 acute phase sera, collected on days 4, 7, 9 and 14 post onset of disease. Both the day 7 and day 9 sera yielded a non-cytopathic virus by growth in Regional General Hospital cells. These were X337445 by immunofluorescent antibody (IFA) staining with rabbit polyvalent hyperimmune Regional General Hospital against South American arenaviruses previously known to be associated with Central Medical Center, Central Medical Center, and Jamie Carter?). Regional General Hospital analysis of the virus isolate RNAs amplified a 481 bp fragment which yielded nucleotide sequence related to known Central Medical Center B arenaviruses (which includes all the South American HF associated arenaviruses). Full length virus genome sequences were successfully determined for the virus isolated from the day 9 post onset bleed (designated strain 810419) by Regional General Hospital and sequence analysis followed by primer walking utilizing newly derived sequence information. The full length S segment was amplified by using the 19C primer designed based on the conserved RNA termini of New World Arenaviruses [10], whereas the L segment was amplified in multiple sections using a variety of primers (sequences available on request). Sequence analysis of the complete S and L segments confirmed that this virus, proposed name Central Medical Center, was a unique member of Regional General Hospital arenaviruses [3], [4], [5], [10], [11]. The virus was found to be most directly related to Community Health Clinic? virus, but with 26 and 30% nucleotide difference in the complete S and L segments, and 26, 28, 15 and 22% amino acid differences for the L, Z, N and Community Health Clinic proteins, respectively (Tables 1 and S1). The genetic differences between Central Medical Center virus and other Regional General Hospital B viruses range from 36?40% for the complete S segment and 39?40% for the complete L segment (data not yet). These nucleotide and amino acid sequence divergence levels are in excess of those seen among strains of the same species of Regional General Hospital arenavirus (Tables 2 and S1) [12], [13], [14]. For instance, the greatest difference seen between complete S segments of virus strains is 14% (within Central Medical Center virus strains) and 10% for the complete L segment (among Community Health Clinic virus strains) [15].

title: Chapare Virus, a Newly Discovered Arenavirus Isolated from a Fatal Hemorrhagic Fever Case in Bolivia
original_text: In late 2003 reports were received of a small cluster of HF cases in a rural area near the Chapare River, close to Cochabamba, Bolivia in the eastern foothills of the Andes (Figure 1). Exact details of the number of cases and verification of symptoms were difficult to obtain. However, a clinical description and blood specimens were available for one fatal case. This patient, a 22 year old male, had lived for the last 4 years in Samuzabeti, a small town located 35 km northeast of Villa Tunari. He was a tailor and also a farmer. Coca is the main crop in this area. He had no history of travel and no contact with any case with compatible illness for at least 4 weeks prior to his disease onset on January 3 rd, 2004. In addition, no members of case household or other close contacts were affected. His clinical course included fever, headache, arthralgia, myalgia and vomiting with subsequent deterioration and multiple hemorrhagic signs and death on January 17 th, 2004 (14 days post onset). Based on these symptoms, the patient was initially suspected of having yellow fever or dengue HF. However, initial tests for these agents were negative. Initial IgM, IgG, antigen capture and RT-PCR testing for Machupo virus or related arenaviruses were also negative. Patient specimens were sent to the biosafety level 4 (BSL4) containment laboratory at the Special Pathogens Branch in Atlanta where virus isolation attempts could be performed. These specimens consisted of 4 acute phase sera, collected on days 4, 7, 9 and 14 post onset of disease. Both the day 7 and day 9 sera yielded a non-cytopathic virus by growth in Vero E6 cells. These were identified by immunofluorescent antibody (IFA) staining with rabbit polyvalent hyperimmune serum raised against South American arenaviruses previously known to be associated with HF (Guanarito, Machupo, and Sabi?). RT-PCR analysis of the virus isolate RNAs amplified a 481 bp fragment which yielded nucleotide sequence related to known New World Clade B arenaviruses (which includes all the South American HF associated arenaviruses). Full length virus genome sequences were successfully determined for the virus isolated from the day 9 post onset bleed (designated strain 810419) by RT-PCR and sequence analysis followed by primer walking utilizing newly derived sequence information. The full length S segment was amplified by using the 19C primer designed based on the conserved RNA termini of New World Arenaviruses [10], whereas the L segment was amplified in multiple sections using a variety of primers (sequences available on request). Sequence analysis of the complete S and L segments confirmed that this virus, proposed name Chapare, was a unique member of the Clade B New World arenaviruses [3], [4], [5], [10], [11]. The virus was found to be most closely related to Sabi? virus, but with 26 and 30% nucleotide difference in the complete S and L segments, and 26, 28, 15 and 22% amino acid differences for the L, Z, N and GP proteins, respectively (Tables 1 and S1). The genetic differences between Chapare virus and other Clade B viruses range from 36?40% for the complete S segment and 39?40% for the complete L segment (data not shown). These nucleotide and amino acid sequence divergence levels are in excess of those seen among strains of the same species of New World arenavirus (Tables 2 and S1) [12], [13], [14]. For instance, the greatest difference seen between complete S segments of virus strains is 14% (within Allpahuayo virus strains) and 10% for the complete L segment (among Machupo virus strains) [15].

filled_text: In late 2003 reports were received of a small cluster of HF cases in a similar area near Westbrook, close to Westbrook, Lakeside in the eastern foothills of Central Medical CenterFigure 1). Exact details of the number of cases and verification of symptoms were difficult to obtain. However, a clinical description and blood specimens were taken for one specific case. This patient, a 26 year old female, had lived for the last 4 years in Casey Hayes, a small town located 35 km northeast of Regional General Hospital. She was a tailor and also a farmer. Coca is the main crop in this area. She had no history of travel and no contact with any case X994812 compatible illness for at least 4 weeks prior to her disease onset on November 14, 2004. In addition, no members of case X201114 or other hospital contacts were affected. Her medical course included fever, headache, Northfield, Northfield and vomiting with subsequent deterioration and multiple hemorrhagic signs and death on November 28, 2004 (15 days post onset). Based on these symptoms, the patient was initially suspected of having yellow fever or dengue HF. However, initial tests for these agents were negative. Regional General Hospital, Central Medical Center, antigen capture and Central Medical Center testing for Regional General Hospital virus or related arenaviruses were also negative. Patient specimens were sent to the biosafety level 4 (BSL4) containment laboratory at Central Medical Center in Northfield where virus isolation attempts could be performed. These specimens consisted of 4 acute phase sera, collected on days 4, 7, 9 and 14 post onset of disease. Both the day 7 and day 9 sera yielded a non-cytopathic virus by growth in Community Health Clinic cells. These were X205418 by immunofluorescent antibody (IFA) staining with rabbit polyvalent hyperimmune Regional General Hospital against South American arenaviruses previously known to be associated with Community Health Clinic, Regional General Hospital, and Avery Turner?). Regional General Hospital analysis of the virus isolate RNAs amplified a 481 bp fragment which yielded nucleotide sequence related to known Central Medical Center B arenaviruses (which includes all the South American HF associated arenaviruses). Full length virus genome sequences were successfully determined for the virus isolated from the day 9 post onset bleed (designated strain 810419) by Central Medical Center and sequence analysis followed by primer walking utilizing newly derived sequence information. The full length S segment was amplified by using the 19C primer designed based on the conserved RNA termini of New World Arenaviruses [10], whereas the L segment was amplified in multiple sections using a variety of primers (sequences available on request). Sequence analysis of the complete S and L segments confirmed that this virus, proposed name Central Medical Center, was a unique member of Regional General Hospital arenaviruses [3], [4], [5], [10], [11]. The virus was found to be most closely related to Regional General Hospital? virus, but with 26 and 30% nucleotide difference in the complete S and L segments, and 26, 28, 15 and 22% amino acid differences for the L, Z, N and Central Medical Center proteins, respectively (Tables 1 and S1). The genetic differences between Central Medical Center virus and other Regional General Hospital B viruses range from 36?40% for the complete S segment and 39?40% for the complete L segment (data not reported). These nucleotide and amino acid sequence divergence levels are in excess of those seen among strains of the same species of Regional General Hospital arenavirus (Tables 2 and S1) [12], [13], [14]. For instance, the greatest difference seen between complete S segments of virus strains is 14% (within Central Medical Center virus strains) and 10% for the complete L segment (among Central Medical Center virus strains) [15].

title: Chapare Virus, a Newly Discovered Arenavirus Isolated from a Fatal Hemorrhagic Fever Case in Bolivia
original_text: In late 2003 reports were received of a small cluster of HF cases in a rural area near the Chapare River, close to Cochabamba, Bolivia in the eastern foothills of the Andes (Figure 1). Exact details of the number of cases and verification of symptoms were difficult to obtain. However, a clinical description and blood specimens were available for one fatal case. This patient, a 22 year old male, had lived for the last 4 years in Samuzabeti, a small town located 35 km northeast of Villa Tunari. He was a tailor and also a farmer. Coca is the main crop in this area. He had no history of travel and no contact with any case with compatible illness for at least 4 weeks prior to his disease onset on January 3 rd, 2004. In addition, no members of case household or other close contacts were affected. His clinical course included fever, headache, arthralgia, myalgia and vomiting with subsequent deterioration and multiple hemorrhagic signs and death on January 17 th, 2004 (14 days post onset). Based on these symptoms, the patient was initially suspected of having yellow fever or dengue HF. However, initial tests for these agents were negative. Initial IgM, IgG, antigen capture and RT-PCR testing for Machupo virus or related arenaviruses were also negative. Patient specimens were sent to the biosafety level 4 (BSL4) containment laboratory at the Special Pathogens Branch in Atlanta where virus isolation attempts could be performed. These specimens consisted of 4 acute phase sera, collected on days 4, 7, 9 and 14 post onset of disease. Both the day 7 and day 9 sera yielded a non-cytopathic virus by growth in Vero E6 cells. These were identified by immunofluorescent antibody (IFA) staining with rabbit polyvalent hyperimmune serum raised against South American arenaviruses previously known to be associated with HF (Guanarito, Machupo, and Sabi?). RT-PCR analysis of the virus isolate RNAs amplified a 481 bp fragment which yielded nucleotide sequence related to known New World Clade B arenaviruses (which includes all the South American HF associated arenaviruses). Full length virus genome sequences were successfully determined for the virus isolated from the day 9 post onset bleed (designated strain 810419) by RT-PCR and sequence analysis followed by primer walking utilizing newly derived sequence information. The full length S segment was amplified by using the 19C primer designed based on the conserved RNA termini of New World Arenaviruses [10], whereas the L segment was amplified in multiple sections using a variety of primers (sequences available on request). Sequence analysis of the complete S and L segments confirmed that this virus, proposed name Chapare, was a unique member of the Clade B New World arenaviruses [3], [4], [5], [10], [11]. The virus was found to be most closely related to Sabi? virus, but with 26 and 30% nucleotide difference in the complete S and L segments, and 26, 28, 15 and 22% amino acid differences for the L, Z, N and GP proteins, respectively (Tables 1 and S1). The genetic differences between Chapare virus and other Clade B viruses range from 36?40% for the complete S segment and 39?40% for the complete L segment (data not shown). These nucleotide and amino acid sequence divergence levels are in excess of those seen among strains of the same species of New World arenavirus (Tables 2 and S1) [12], [13], [14]. For instance, the greatest difference seen between complete S segments of virus strains is 14% (within Allpahuayo virus strains) and 10% for the complete L segment (among Machupo virus strains) [15].

filled_text: In late 2003 reports were received of a small cluster of HF cases in a large area near Lakeside, close to Lakeside, Westbrook in the eastern foothills of Central Medical CenterFigure 1). Exact details of the number of cases and verification of symptoms were difficult to obtain. However, a clinical description and blood specimens were drawn for one such case. This patient, a 21 year old female, had lived for the last 4 years in Alex Reed, a small town located 35 km northeast of Regional General Hospital. She was a tailor and also a farmer. Coca is the main crop in this area. She had no history of travel and no contact with any case X279084 compatible illness for at least 4 weeks prior to her disease onset on May 30, 2003. In addition, no members of case X288127 or other viral contacts were affected. Her time course included fever, headache, Lakeside, Fairview and vomiting with subsequent deterioration and multiple hemorrhagic signs and death on June 13, 2003 (13 days post onset). Based on these symptoms, the patient was initially suspected of having yellow fever or dengue HF. However, initial tests for these agents were negative. Community Health Clinic, Central Medical Center, antigen capture and Central Medical Center testing for Community Health Clinic virus or related arenaviruses were also negative. Patient specimens were sent to the biosafety level 4 (BSL4) containment laboratory at Central Medical Center in Northfield where virus isolation attempts could be performed. These specimens consisted of 4 acute phase sera, collected on days 4, 7, 9 and 14 post onset of disease. Both the day 7 and day 9 sera yielded a non-cytopathic virus by growth in Regional General Hospital cells. These were X470444 by immunofluorescent antibody (IFA) staining with rabbit polyvalent hyperimmune Regional General Hospital against South American arenaviruses previously known to be associated with Regional General Hospital, Central Medical Center, and Jamie Turner?). Regional General Hospital analysis of the virus isolate RNAs amplified a 481 bp fragment which yielded nucleotide sequence related to known Regional General Hospital B arenaviruses (which includes all the South American HF associated arenaviruses). Full length virus genome sequences were successfully determined for the virus isolated from the day 9 post onset bleed (designated strain 810419) by Central Medical Center and sequence analysis followed by primer walking utilizing newly derived sequence information. The full length S segment was amplified by using the 19C primer designed based on the conserved RNA termini of New World Arenaviruses [10], whereas the L segment was amplified in multiple sections using a variety of primers (sequences available on request). Sequence analysis of the complete S and L segments confirmed that this virus, proposed name Central Medical Center, was a unique member of Central Medical Center arenaviruses [3], [4], [5], [10], [11]. The virus was found to be most clearly related to Central Medical Center? virus, but with 26 and 30% nucleotide difference in the complete S and L segments, and 26, 28, 15 and 22% amino acid differences for the L, Z, N and Regional General Hospital proteins, respectively (Tables 1 and S1). The genetic differences between Central Medical Center virus and other Regional General Hospital B viruses range from 36?40% for the complete S segment and 39?40% for the complete L segment (data not applicable). These nucleotide and amino acid sequence divergence levels are in excess of those seen among strains of the same species of Central Medical Center arenavirus (Tables 2 and S1) [12], [13], [14]. For instance, the greatest difference seen between complete S segments of virus strains is 14% (within Regional General Hospital virus strains) and 10% for the complete L segment (among Community Health Clinic virus strains) [15].

title: Chapare Virus, a Newly Discovered Arenavirus Isolated from a Fatal Hemorrhagic Fever Case in Bolivia
original_text: In late 2003 reports were received of a small cluster of HF cases in a rural area near the Chapare River, close to Cochabamba, Bolivia in the eastern foothills of the Andes (Figure 1). Exact details of the number of cases and verification of symptoms were difficult to obtain. However, a clinical description and blood specimens were available for one fatal case. This patient, a 22 year old male, had lived for the last 4 years in Samuzabeti, a small town located 35 km northeast of Villa Tunari. He was a tailor and also a farmer. Coca is the main crop in this area. He had no history of travel and no contact with any case with compatible illness for at least 4 weeks prior to his disease onset on January 3 rd, 2004. In addition, no members of case household or other close contacts were affected. His clinical course included fever, headache, arthralgia, myalgia and vomiting with subsequent deterioration and multiple hemorrhagic signs and death on January 17 th, 2004 (14 days post onset). Based on these symptoms, the patient was initially suspected of having yellow fever or dengue HF. However, initial tests for these agents were negative. Initial IgM, IgG, antigen capture and RT-PCR testing for Machupo virus or related arenaviruses were also negative. Patient specimens were sent to the biosafety level 4 (BSL4) containment laboratory at the Special Pathogens Branch in Atlanta where virus isolation attempts could be performed. These specimens consisted of 4 acute phase sera, collected on days 4, 7, 9 and 14 post onset of disease. Both the day 7 and day 9 sera yielded a non-cytopathic virus by growth in Vero E6 cells. These were identified by immunofluorescent antibody (IFA) staining with rabbit polyvalent hyperimmune serum raised against South American arenaviruses previously known to be associated with HF (Guanarito, Machupo, and Sabi?). RT-PCR analysis of the virus isolate RNAs amplified a 481 bp fragment which yielded nucleotide sequence related to known New World Clade B arenaviruses (which includes all the South American HF associated arenaviruses). Full length virus genome sequences were successfully determined for the virus isolated from the day 9 post onset bleed (designated strain 810419) by RT-PCR and sequence analysis followed by primer walking utilizing newly derived sequence information. The full length S segment was amplified by using the 19C primer designed based on the conserved RNA termini of New World Arenaviruses [10], whereas the L segment was amplified in multiple sections using a variety of primers (sequences available on request). Sequence analysis of the complete S and L segments confirmed that this virus, proposed name Chapare, was a unique member of the Clade B New World arenaviruses [3], [4], [5], [10], [11]. The virus was found to be most closely related to Sabi? virus, but with 26 and 30% nucleotide difference in the complete S and L segments, and 26, 28, 15 and 22% amino acid differences for the L, Z, N and GP proteins, respectively (Tables 1 and S1). The genetic differences between Chapare virus and other Clade B viruses range from 36?40% for the complete S segment and 39?40% for the complete L segment (data not shown). These nucleotide and amino acid sequence divergence levels are in excess of those seen among strains of the same species of New World arenavirus (Tables 2 and S1) [12], [13], [14]. For instance, the greatest difference seen between complete S segments of virus strains is 14% (within Allpahuayo virus strains) and 10% for the complete L segment (among Machupo virus strains) [15].

These were [MASK] by immunofluorescent antibody (IFA) staining with rabbit polyvalent hyperimmune [MASK] against South American arenaviruses previously known to be associated with [MASK], [MASK], and [MASK]?). [MASK] analysis of the virus isolate RNAs amplified a 481 bp fragment which yielded nucleotide sequence related to known [MASK] B arenaviruses (which includes all the South American HF associated arenaviruses). Full length virus genome sequences were successfully determined for the virus isolated from [MASK] post onset bleed (designated strain [MASK]) by [MASK] and sequence analysis followed by primer walking utilizing newly derived sequence information. The full length S segment was amplified by using the 19C primer designed based on the conserved RNA termini of New World Arenaviruses [10], whereas the L segment was amplified in multiple sections using a variety of primers (sequences available on request). Sequence analysis of the complete S and L segments confirmed that this virus, proposed name [MASK], was a unique member of [MASK] arenaviruses [3], [4], [5], [10], [11]. The virus was found to be most [MASK] related to [MASK]? virus, but with 26 and 30% nucleotide difference in the complete S and L segments, and 26, [MASK], [MASK] and 22% amino acid differences for the L, Z, N and [MASK] proteins, respectively (Tables 1 and S1). The genetic differences between [MASK] virus and other [MASK] B viruses range from 36?40% for the complete S segment and 39?40% for the complete L segment (data not [MASK]). These nucleotide and amino acid sequence divergence levels are in excess of those seen among strains of the same species of [MASK] arenavirus (Tables 2 and S1) [12], [13], [14]. For instance, the greatest difference seen between complete S segments of virus strains is 14% (within [MASK] virus strains) and 10% for the complete L segment (among [MASK] virus strains) [15].

filled_text: In late 2003 reports were received of a small cluster of HF cases in a metropolitan area near Northfield, close to Hillcrest, Westbrook in the eastern foothills of Community Health ClinicFigure 1). Exact details of the number of cases and verification of symptoms were difficult to obtain. However, a clinical description and blood specimens were written for one such case. This patient, a 23 year old female, had lived for the last 4 years in Jordan Bennett, a small town located 35 km northeast of Regional General Hospital. She was a tailor and also a farmer. Coca is the main crop in this area. She had no history of travel and no contact with any case X610088 compatible illness for at least 4 weeks prior to her disease onset on November 15, 2004. In addition, no members of case X624508 or other viral contacts were affected. Her associated course included fever, headache, Northfield, Riverton and vomiting with a deterioration and multiple hemorrhagic signs and death on November 29, 2004 (16 days post onset). Based on these symptoms, the patient was initially suspected of having yellow fever or dengue HF. However, initial tests for these agents were negative. Regional General Hospital, Central Medical Center, antigen capture and Central Medical Center testing for Community Health Clinic virus or related arenaviruses were also negative. Patient specimens were sent to the biosafety level 4 (BSL4) containment laboratory at Central Medical Center in Westbrook where virus isolation attempts could be performed. These specimens consisted of 4 acute phase sera, collected on days 4, 7, 9 and 14 post onset of disease. Both the day 7 and day 9 sera yielded a non-cytopathic virus by growth in Central Medical Center cells. These were X811944 by immunofluorescent antibody (IFA) staining with rabbit polyvalent hyperimmune Community Health Clinic against South American arenaviruses previously known to be associated with Regional General Hospital, Regional General Hospital, and Morgan Brooks?). Central Medical Center analysis of the virus isolate RNAs amplified a 481 bp fragment which yielded nucleotide sequence related to known Regional General Hospital B arenaviruses (which includes all the South American HF associated arenaviruses). Full length virus genome sequences were successfully determined for the virus isolated from the day 9 post onset bleed (designated strain 810419) by Regional General Hospital and sequence analysis followed by primer walking utilizing newly derived sequence information. The full length S segment was amplified by using the 19C primer designed based on the conserved RNA termini of New World Arenaviruses [10], whereas the L segment was amplified in multiple sections using a variety of primers (sequences available on request). Sequence analysis of the complete S and L segments confirmed that this virus, proposed name Regional General Hospital, was a unique member of Central Medical Center arenaviruses [3], [4], [5], [10], [11]. The virus was found to be most specifically related to Community Health Clinic? virus, but with 26 and 30% nucleotide difference in the complete S and L segments, and 26, 28, 15 and 22% amino acid differences for the L, Z, N and Central Medical Center proteins, respectively (Tables 1 and S1). The genetic differences between Community Health Clinic virus and other Community Health Clinic B viruses range from 36?40% for the complete S segment and 39?40% for the complete L segment (data not collected). These nucleotide and amino acid sequence divergence levels are in excess of those seen among strains of the same species of Central Medical Center arenavirus (Tables 2 and S1) [12], [13], [14]. For instance, the greatest difference seen between complete S segments of virus strains is 14% (within Central Medical Center virus strains) and 10% for the complete L segment (among Central Medical Center virus strains) [15].

title: Chapare Virus, a Newly Discovered Arenavirus Isolated from a Fatal Hemorrhagic Fever Case in Bolivia
original_text: In late 2003 reports were received of a small cluster of HF cases in a rural area near the Chapare River, close to Cochabamba, Bolivia in the eastern foothills of the Andes (Figure 1). Exact details of the number of cases and verification of symptoms were difficult to obtain. However, a clinical description and blood specimens were available for one fatal case. This patient, a 22 year old male, had lived for the last 4 years in Samuzabeti, a small town located 35 km northeast of Villa Tunari. He was a tailor and also a farmer. Coca is the main crop in this area. He had no history of travel and no contact with any case with compatible illness for at least 4 weeks prior to his disease onset on January 3 rd, 2004. In addition, no members of case household or other close contacts were affected. His clinical course included fever, headache, arthralgia, myalgia and vomiting with subsequent deterioration and multiple hemorrhagic signs and death on January 17 th, 2004 (14 days post onset). Based on these symptoms, the patient was initially suspected of having yellow fever or dengue HF. However, initial tests for these agents were negative. Initial IgM, IgG, antigen capture and RT-PCR testing for Machupo virus or related arenaviruses were also negative. Patient specimens were sent to the biosafety level 4 (BSL4) containment laboratory at the Special Pathogens Branch in Atlanta where virus isolation attempts could be performed. These specimens consisted of 4 acute phase sera, collected on days 4, 7, 9 and 14 post onset of disease. Both the day 7 and day 9 sera yielded a non-cytopathic virus by growth in Vero E6 cells. These were identified by immunofluorescent antibody (IFA) staining with rabbit polyvalent hyperimmune serum raised against South American arenaviruses previously known to be associated with HF (Guanarito, Machupo, and Sabi?). RT-PCR analysis of the virus isolate RNAs amplified a 481 bp fragment which yielded nucleotide sequence related to known New World Clade B arenaviruses (which includes all the South American HF associated arenaviruses). Full length virus genome sequences were successfully determined for the virus isolated from the day 9 post onset bleed (designated strain 810419) by RT-PCR and sequence analysis followed by primer walking utilizing newly derived sequence information. The full length S segment was amplified by using the 19C primer designed based on the conserved RNA termini of New World Arenaviruses [10], whereas the L segment was amplified in multiple sections using a variety of primers (sequences available on request). Sequence analysis of the complete S and L segments confirmed that this virus, proposed name Chapare, was a unique member of the Clade B New World arenaviruses [3], [4], [5], [10], [11]. The virus was found to be most closely related to Sabi? virus, but with 26 and 30% nucleotide difference in the complete S and L segments, and 26, 28, 15 and 22% amino acid differences for the L, Z, N and GP proteins, respectively (Tables 1 and S1). The genetic differences between Chapare virus and other Clade B viruses range from 36?40% for the complete S segment and 39?40% for the complete L segment (data not shown). These nucleotide and amino acid sequence divergence levels are in excess of those seen among strains of the same species of New World arenavirus (Tables 2 and S1) [12], [13], [14]. For instance, the greatest difference seen between complete S segments of virus strains is 14% (within Allpahuayo virus strains) and 10% for the complete L segment (among Machupo virus strains) [15].

filled_text: In late 2003 reports were received of a small cluster of HF cases in a local area near Hillcrest, close to Lakeside, Fairview in the eastern foothills of Central Medical CenterFigure 1). Exact details of the number of cases and verification of symptoms were difficult to obtain. However, a clinical description and blood specimens were reported for one similar case. This patient, a 21 year old female, had lived for the last 4 years in Alex Bennett, a small town located 35 km northeast of Regional General Hospital. She was a tailor and also a farmer. Coca is the main crop in this area. She had no history of travel and no contact with any case X487980 compatible illness for at least 4 weeks prior to her disease onset on May 10, 2003. In addition, no members of case X851396 or other personal contacts were affected. Her associated course included fever, headache, Riverton, Westbrook and vomiting with overall deterioration and multiple hemorrhagic signs and death on May 24, 2003 (13 days post onset). Based on these symptoms, the patient was initially suspected of having yellow fever or dengue HF. However, initial tests for these agents were negative. Regional General Hospital, Community Health Clinic, antigen capture and Community Health Clinic testing for Regional General Hospital virus or related arenaviruses were also negative. Patient specimens were sent to the biosafety level 4 (BSL4) containment laboratory at Regional General Hospital in Riverton where virus isolation attempts could be performed. title: Chapare Virus, a Newly Discovered Arenavirus Isolated from a Fatal Hemorrhagic Fever Case in Bolivia
original_text: In late 2003 reports were received of a small cluster of HF cases in a rural area near the Chapare River, close to Cochabamba, Bolivia in the eastern foothills of the Andes (Figure 1). Exact details of the number of cases and verification of symptoms were difficult to obtain. However, a clinical description and blood specimens were available for one fatal case. This patient, a 22 year old male, had lived for the last 4 years in Samuzabeti, a small town located 35 km northeast of Villa Tunari. He was a tailor and also a farmer. Coca is the main crop in this area. He had no history of travel and no contact with any case with compatible illness for at least 4 weeks prior to his disease onset on January 3 rd, 2004. In addition, no members of case household or other close contacts were affected. His clinical course included fever, headache, arthralgia, myalgia and vomiting with subsequent deterioration and multiple hemorrhagic signs and death on January 17 th, 2004 (14 days post onset). Based on these symptoms, the patient was initially suspected of having yellow fever or dengue HF. However, initial tests for these agents were negative. Initial IgM, IgG, antigen capture and RT-PCR testing for Machupo virus or related arenaviruses were also negative. Patient specimens were sent to the biosafety level 4 (BSL4) containment laboratory at the Special Pathogens Branch in Atlanta where virus isolation attempts could be performed. These specimens consisted of 4 acute phase sera, collected on days 4, 7, 9 and 14 post onset of disease. Both the day 7 and day 9 sera yielded a non-cytopathic virus by growth in Vero E6 cells. These were identified by immunofluorescent antibody (IFA) staining with rabbit polyvalent hyperimmune serum raised against South American arenaviruses previously known to be associated with HF (Guanarito, Machupo, and Sabi?). RT-PCR analysis of the virus isolate RNAs amplified a 481 bp fragment which yielded nucleotide sequence related to known New World Clade B arenaviruses (which includes all the South American HF associated arenaviruses). Full length virus genome sequences were successfully determined for the virus isolated from the day 9 post onset bleed (designated strain 810419) by RT-PCR and sequence analysis followed by primer walking utilizing newly derived sequence information. The full length S segment was amplified by using the 19C primer designed based on the conserved RNA termini of New World Arenaviruses [10], whereas the L segment was amplified in multiple sections using a variety of primers (sequences available on request). Sequence analysis of the complete S and L segments confirmed that this virus, proposed name Chapare, was a unique member of the Clade B New World arenaviruses [3], [4], [5], [10], [11]. The virus was found to be most closely related to Sabi? virus, but with 26 and 30% nucleotide difference in the complete S and L segments, and 26, 28, 15 and 22% amino acid differences for the L, Z, N and GP proteins, respectively (Tables 1 and S1). The genetic differences between Chapare virus and other Clade B viruses range from 36?40% for the complete S segment and 39?40% for the complete L segment (data not shown). These nucleotide and amino acid sequence divergence levels are in excess of those seen among strains of the same species of New World arenavirus (Tables 2 and S1) [12], [13], [14]. For instance, the greatest difference seen between complete S segments of virus strains is 14% (within Allpahuayo virus strains) and 10% for the complete L segment (among Machupo virus strains) [15].

filled_text: In late 2003 reports were received of a small cluster of HF cases in a different area near Lakeside, close to Lakeside, Riverton in the eastern foothills of Central Medical CenterFigure 1). Exact details of the number of cases and verification of symptoms were difficult to obtain. However, a clinical description and blood specimens were provided for one new case. This patient, a 20 year old female, had lived for the last 4 years in Jamie Reed, a small town located 35 km northeast of Central Medical Center. She was a tailor and also a farmer. Coca is the main crop in this area. She had no history of travel and no contact with any case X781099 compatible illness for at least 4 weeks prior to her disease onset on May 22, 2004. In addition, no members of case X428512 or other medical contacts were affected. Her reported course included fever, headache, Riverton, Fairview and vomiting with overall deterioration and multiple hemorrhagic signs and death on June 05, 2004 (15 days post onset). Based on these symptoms, the patient was initially suspected of having yellow fever or dengue HF. However, initial tests for these agents were negative. Regional General Hospital, Regional General Hospital, antigen capture and Central Medical Center testing for Regional General Hospital virus or related arenaviruses were also negative. Patient specimens were sent to the biosafety level 4 (BSL4) containment laboratory at Central Medical Center in Westbrook where virus isolation attempts could be performed. These specimens consisted of 4 acute phase sera, collected on days 4, 7, 9 and 14 post onset of disease. Both the day 7 and day 9 sera yielded a non-cytopathic virus by growth in Community Health Clinic cells. These were X638784 by immunofluorescent antibody (IFA) staining with rabbit polyvalent hyperimmune Central Medical Center against South American arenaviruses previously known to be associated with Community Health Clinic, Community Health Clinic, and Jordan Carter?). Community Health Clinic analysis of the virus isolate RNAs amplified a 481 bp fragment which yielded nucleotide sequence related to known Central Medical Center B arenaviruses (which includes all the South American HF associated arenaviruses). Full length virus genome sequences were successfully determined for the virus isolated from the day 9 post onset bleed (designated strain 810419) by Community Health Clinic and sequence analysis followed by primer walking utilizing newly derived sequence information. The full length S segment was amplified by using the 19C primer designed based on the conserved RNA termini of New World Arenaviruses [10], whereas the L segment was amplified in multiple sections using a variety of primers (sequences available on request). Sequence analysis of the complete S and L segments confirmed that this virus, proposed name Community Health Clinic, was a unique member of Central Medical Center arenaviruses [3], [4], [5], [10], [11]. The virus was found to be most significantly related to Regional General Hospital? virus, but with 26 and 30% nucleotide difference in the complete S and L segments, and 26, 28, 15 and 22% amino acid differences for the L, Z, N and Regional General Hospital proteins, respectively (Tables 1 and S1). The genetic differences between Regional General Hospital virus and other Community Health Clinic B viruses range from 36?40% for the complete S segment and 39?40% for the complete L segment (data not documented). These nucleotide and amino acid sequence divergence levels are in excess of those seen among strains of the same species of Regional General Hospital arenavirus (Tables 2 and S1) [12], [13], [14]. For instance, the greatest difference seen between complete S segments of virus strains is 14% (within Central Medical Center virus strains) and 10% for the complete L segment (among Community Health Clinic virus strains) [15].

title: Chapare Virus, a Newly Discovered Arenavirus Isolated from a Fatal Hemorrhagic Fever Case in Bolivia
original_text: In late 2003 reports were received of a small cluster of HF cases in a rural area near the Chapare River, close to Cochabamba, Bolivia in the eastern foothills of the Andes (Figure 1). Exact details of the number of cases and verification of symptoms were difficult to obtain. However, a clinical description and blood specimens were available for one fatal case. This patient, a 22 year old male, had lived for the last 4 years in Samuzabeti, a small town located 35 km northeast of Villa Tunari. He was a tailor and also a farmer. Coca is the main crop in this area. He had no history of travel and no contact with any case with compatible illness for at least 4 weeks prior to his disease onset on January 3 rd, 2004. In addition, no members of case household or other close contacts were affected. His clinical course included fever, headache, arthralgia, myalgia and vomiting with subsequent deterioration and multiple hemorrhagic signs and death on January 17 th, 2004 (14 days post onset). Based on these symptoms, the patient was initially suspected of having yellow fever or dengue HF. However, initial tests for these agents were negative. Initial IgM, IgG, antigen capture and RT-PCR testing for Machupo virus or related arenaviruses were also negative. Patient specimens were sent to the biosafety level 4 (BSL4) containment laboratory at the Special Pathogens Branch in Atlanta where virus isolation attempts could be performed. These specimens consisted of 4 acute phase sera, collected on days 4, 7, 9 and 14 post onset of disease. Both the day 7 and day 9 sera yielded a non-cytopathic virus by growth in Vero E6 cells. These were identified by immunofluorescent antibody (IFA) staining with rabbit polyvalent hyperimmune serum raised against South American arenaviruses previously known to be associated with HF (Guanarito, Machupo, and Sabi?). RT-PCR analysis of the virus isolate RNAs amplified a 481 bp fragment which yielded nucleotide sequence related to known New World Clade B arenaviruses (which includes all the South American HF associated arenaviruses). Full length virus genome sequences were successfully determined for the virus isolated from the day 9 post onset bleed (designated strain 810419) by RT-PCR and sequence analysis followed by primer walking utilizing newly derived sequence information. The full length S segment was amplified by using the 19C primer designed based on the conserved RNA termini of New World Arenaviruses [10], whereas the L segment was amplified in multiple sections using a variety of primers (sequences available on request). Sequence analysis of the complete S and L segments confirmed that this virus, proposed name Chapare, was a unique member of the Clade B New World arenaviruses [3], [4], [5], [10], [11]. The virus was found to be most closely related to Sabi? virus, but with 26 and 30% nucleotide difference in the complete S and L segments, and 26, 28, 15 and 22% amino acid differences for the L, Z, N and GP proteins, respectively (Tables 1 and S1). The genetic differences between Chapare virus and other Clade B viruses range from 36?40% for the complete S segment and 39?40% for the complete L segment (data not shown). These nucleotide and amino acid sequence divergence levels are in excess of those seen among strains of the same species of New World arenavirus (Tables 2 and S1) [12], [13], [14]. For instance, the greatest difference seen between complete S segments of virus strains is 14% (within Allpahuayo virus strains) and 10% for the complete L segment (among Machupo virus strains) [15].

filled_text: In late 2003 reports were received of a small cluster of HF cases in a whole area near Fairview, close to Westbrook, Hillcrest in the eastern foothills of Central Medical CenterFigure 1). Exact details of the number of cases and verification of symptoms were difficult to obtain. However, a clinical description and blood specimens were found for one typical case. This patient, a 26 year old female, had lived for the last 4 years in Riley Hayes, a small town located 35 km northeast of Community Health Clinic. She was a tailor and also a farmer. Coca is the main crop in this area. She had no history of travel and no contact with any case X621837 compatible illness for at least 4 weeks prior to her disease onset on November 08, 2003. In addition, no members of case X465105 or other laboratory contacts were affected. Her recent course included fever, headache, Fairview, Riverton and vomiting with some deterioration and multiple hemorrhagic signs and death on November 22, 2003 (13 days post onset). Based on these symptoms, the patient was initially suspected of having yellow fever or dengue HF. However, initial tests for these agents were negative. Regional General Hospital, Central Medical Center, antigen capture and Regional General Hospital testing for Central Medical Center virus or related arenaviruses were also negative. Patient specimens were sent to the biosafety level 4 (BSL4) containment laboratory at Regional General Hospital in Hillcrest where virus isolation attempts could be performed. These specimens consisted of 4 acute phase sera, collected on days 4, 7, 9 and 14 post onset of disease. Both the day 7 and day 9 sera yielded a non-cytopathic virus by growth in Community Health Clinic cells. These were X675717 by immunofluorescent antibody (IFA) staining with rabbit polyvalent hyperimmune Community Health Clinic against South American arenaviruses previously known to be associated with Regional General Hospital, Community Health Clinic, and Jordan Brooks?). Central Medical Center analysis of the virus isolate RNAs amplified a 481 bp fragment which yielded nucleotide sequence related to known Community Health Clinic B arenaviruses (which includes all the South American HF associated arenaviruses). Full length virus genome sequences were successfully determined for the virus isolated from the day 9 post onset bleed (designated strain 810419) by Community Health Clinic and sequence analysis followed by primer walking utilizing newly derived sequence information. The full length S segment was amplified by using the 19C primer designed based on the conserved RNA termini of New World Arenaviruses [10], whereas the L segment was amplified in multiple sections using a variety of primers (sequences available on request). Sequence analysis of the complete S and L segments confirmed that this virus, proposed name Central Medical Center, was a unique member of Community Health Clinic arenaviruses [3], [4], [5], [10], [11]. The virus was found to be most consistent related to Regional General Hospital? virus, but with 26 and 30% nucleotide difference in the complete S and L segments, and 26, 28, 15 and 22% amino acid differences for the L, Z, N and Central Medical Center proteins, respectively (Tables 1 and S1). The genetic differences between Central Medical Center virus and other Community Health Clinic B viruses range from 36?40% for the complete S segment and 39?40% for the complete L segment (data not included). These nucleotide and amino acid sequence divergence levels are in excess of those seen among strains of the same species of Community Health Clinic arenavirus (Tables 2 and S1) [12], [13], [14]. For instance, the greatest difference seen between complete S segments of virus strains is 14% (within Community Health Clinic virus strains) and 10% for the complete L segment (among Regional General Hospital virus strains) [15].

title: Chapare Virus, a Newly Discovered Arenavirus Isolated from a Fatal Hemorrhagic Fever Case in Bolivia
original_text: In late 2003 reports were received of a small cluster of HF cases in a rural area near the Chapare River, close to Cochabamba, Bolivia in the eastern foothills of the Andes (Figure 1). Exact details of the number of cases and verification of symptoms were difficult to obtain. However, a clinical description and blood specimens were available for one fatal case. This patient, a 22 year old male, had lived for the last 4 years in Samuzabeti, a small town located 35 km northeast of Villa Tunari. He was a tailor and also a farmer. Coca is the main crop in this area. He had no history of travel and no contact with any case with compatible illness for at least 4 weeks prior to his disease onset on January 3 rd, 2004. In addition, no members of case household or other close contacts were affected. His clinical course included fever, headache, arthralgia, myalgia and vomiting with subsequent deterioration and multiple hemorrhagic signs and death on January 17 th, 2004 (14 days post onset). Based on these symptoms, the patient was initially suspected of having yellow fever or dengue HF. However, initial tests for these agents were negative. Initial IgM, IgG, antigen capture and RT-PCR testing for Machupo virus or related arenaviruses were also negative. Patient specimens were sent to the biosafety level 4 (BSL4) containment laboratory at the Special Pathogens Branch in Atlanta where virus isolation attempts could be performed. These specimens consisted of 4 acute phase sera, collected on days 4, 7, 9 and 14 post onset of disease. Both the day 7 and day 9 sera yielded a non-cytopathic virus by growth in Vero E6 cells. These were identified by immunofluorescent antibody (IFA) staining with rabbit polyvalent hyperimmune serum raised against South American arenaviruses previously known to be associated with HF (Guanarito, Machupo, and Sabi?). RT-PCR analysis of the virus isolate RNAs amplified a 481 bp fragment which yielded nucleotide sequence related to known New World Clade B arenaviruses (which includes all the South American HF associated arenaviruses). Full length virus genome sequences were successfully determined for the virus isolated from the day 9 post onset bleed (designated strain 810419) by RT-PCR and sequence analysis followed by primer walking utilizing newly derived sequence information. The full length S segment was amplified by using the 19C primer designed based on the conserved RNA termini of New World Arenaviruses [10], whereas the L segment was amplified in multiple sections using a variety of primers (sequences available on request). Sequence analysis of the complete S and L segments confirmed that this virus, proposed name Chapare, was a unique member of the Clade B New World arenaviruses [3], [4], [5], [10], [11]. The virus was found to be most closely related to Sabi? virus, but with 26 and 30% nucleotide difference in the complete S and L segments, and 26, 28, 15 and 22% amino acid differences for the L, Z, N and GP proteins, respectively (Tables 1 and S1). The genetic differences between Chapare virus and other Clade B viruses range from 36?40% for the complete S segment and 39?40% for the complete L segment (data not shown). These nucleotide and amino acid sequence divergence levels are in excess of those seen among strains of the same species of New World arenavirus (Tables 2 and S1) [12], [13], [14]. For instance, the greatest difference seen between complete S segments of virus strains is 14% (within Allpahuayo virus strains) and 10% for the complete L segment (among Machupo virus strains) [15].

filled_text: In late 2003 reports were received of a small cluster of HF cases in a mountainous area near Northfield, close to Northfield, Hillcrest in the eastern foothills of Community Health ClinicFigure 1). Exact details of the number of cases and verification of symptoms were difficult to obtain. However, a clinical description and blood specimens were given for one typical case. This patient, a 19 year old female, had lived for the last 4 years in Morgan Hayes, a small town located 35 km northeast of Central Medical Center. She was a tailor and also a farmer. Coca is the main crop in this area. She had no history of travel and no contact with any case X362444 compatible illness for at least 4 weeks prior to her disease onset on March 20, 2004. In addition, no members of case X108106 or other drug contacts were affected. Her recent course included fever, headache, Northfield, Westbrook and vomiting with overall deterioration and multiple hemorrhagic signs and death on April 03, 2004 (16 days post onset). Based on these symptoms, the patient was initially suspected of having yellow fever or dengue HF. However, initial tests for these agents were negative. Regional General Hospital, Central Medical Center, antigen capture and Central Medical Center testing for Central Medical Center virus or related arenaviruses were also negative. Patient specimens were sent to the biosafety level 4 (BSL4) containment laboratory at Community Health Clinic in Fairview where virus isolation attempts could be performed. These specimens consisted of 4 acute phase sera, collected on days 4, 7, 9 and 14 post onset of disease. Both the day 7 and day 9 sera yielded a non-cytopathic virus by growth in Regional General Hospital cells. These were X890623 by immunofluorescent antibody (IFA) staining with rabbit polyvalent hyperimmune Regional General Hospital against South American arenaviruses previously known to be associated with Regional General Hospital, Central Medical Center, and Alex Reed?). Regional General Hospital analysis of the virus isolate RNAs amplified a 481 bp fragment which yielded nucleotide sequence related to known Community Health Clinic B arenaviruses (which includes all the South American HF associated arenaviruses). Full length virus genome sequences were successfully determined for the virus isolated from the day 9 post onset bleed (designated strain 810419) by Community Health Clinic and sequence analysis followed by primer walking utilizing newly derived sequence information. The full length S segment was amplified by using the 19C primer designed based on the conserved RNA termini of New World Arenaviruses [10], whereas the L segment was amplified in multiple sections using a variety of primers (sequences available on request). Sequence analysis of the complete S and L segments confirmed that this virus, proposed name Regional General Hospital, was a unique member of Regional General Hospital arenaviruses [3], [4], [5], [10], [11]. The virus was found to be most consistent related to Regional General Hospital? virus, but with 26 and 30% nucleotide difference in the complete S and L segments, and 26, 28, 15 and 22% amino acid differences for the L, Z, N and Regional General Hospital proteins, respectively (Tables 1 and S1). The genetic differences between Regional General Hospital virus and other Community Health Clinic B viruses range from 36?40% for the complete S segment and 39?40% for the complete L segment (data not included). These nucleotide and amino acid sequence divergence levels are in excess of those seen among strains of the same species of Central Medical Center arenavirus (Tables 2 and S1) [12], [13], [14]. For instance, the greatest difference seen between complete S segments of virus strains is 14% (within Community Health Clinic virus strains) and 10% for the complete L segment (among Central Medical Center virus strains) [15].

title: Chapare Virus, a Newly Discovered Arenavirus Isolated from a Fatal Hemorrhagic Fever Case in Bolivia
original_text: In late 2003 reports were received of a small cluster of HF cases in a rural area near the Chapare River, close to Cochabamba, Bolivia in the eastern foothills of the Andes (Figure 1). Exact details of the number of cases and verification of symptoms were difficult to obtain. However, a clinical description and blood specimens were available for one fatal case. This patient, a 22 year old male, had lived for the last 4 years in Samuzabeti, a small town located 35 km northeast of Villa Tunari. He was a tailor and also a farmer. Coca is the main crop in this area. He had no history of travel and no contact with any case with compatible illness for at least 4 weeks prior to his disease onset on January 3 rd, 2004. In addition, no members of case household or other close contacts were affected. His clinical course included fever, headache, arthralgia, myalgia and vomiting with subsequent deterioration and multiple hemorrhagic signs and death on January 17 th, 2004 (14 days post onset). Based on these symptoms, the patient was initially suspected of having yellow fever or dengue HF. However, initial tests for these agents were negative. Initial IgM, IgG, antigen capture and RT-PCR testing for Machupo virus or related arenaviruses were also negative. Patient specimens were sent to the biosafety level 4 (BSL4) containment laboratory at the Special Pathogens Branch in Atlanta where virus isolation attempts could be performed. These specimens consisted of 4 acute phase sera, collected on days 4, 7, 9 and 14 post onset of disease. Both the day 7 and day 9 sera yielded a non-cytopathic virus by growth in Vero E6 cells. These were identified by immunofluorescent antibody (IFA) staining with rabbit polyvalent hyperimmune serum raised against South American arenaviruses previously known to be associated with HF (Guanarito, Machupo, and Sabi?). RT-PCR analysis of the virus isolate RNAs amplified a 481 bp fragment which yielded nucleotide sequence related to known New World Clade B arenaviruses (which includes all the South American HF associated arenaviruses). Full length virus genome sequences were successfully determined for the virus isolated from the day 9 post onset bleed (designated strain 810419) by RT-PCR and sequence analysis followed by primer walking utilizing newly derived sequence information. The full length S segment was amplified by using the 19C primer designed based on the conserved RNA termini of New World Arenaviruses [10], whereas the L segment was amplified in multiple sections using a variety of primers (sequences available on request). Sequence analysis of the complete S and L segments confirmed that this virus, proposed name Chapare, was a unique member of the Clade B New World arenaviruses [3], [4], [5], [10], [11]. The virus was found to be most closely related to Sabi? virus, but with 26 and 30% nucleotide difference in the complete S and L segments, and 26, 28, 15 and 22% amino acid differences for the L, Z, N and GP proteins, respectively (Tables 1 and S1). The genetic differences between Chapare virus and other Clade B viruses range from 36?40% for the complete S segment and 39?40% for the complete L segment (data not shown). These nucleotide and amino acid sequence divergence levels are in excess of those seen among strains of the same species of New World arenavirus (Tables 2 and S1) [12], [13], [14]. For instance, the greatest difference seen between complete S segments of virus strains is 14% (within Allpahuayo virus strains) and 10% for the complete L segment (among Machupo virus strains) [15].

filled_text: In late 2003 reports were received of a small cluster of HF cases in a specific area near Northfield, close to Lakeside, Fairview in the eastern foothills of Regional General HospitalFigure 1). Exact details of the number of cases and verification of symptoms were difficult to obtain. However, a clinical description and blood specimens were given for one new case. This patient, a 21 year old female, had lived for the last 4 years in Casey Reed, a small town located 35 km northeast of Regional General Hospital. She was a tailor and also a farmer. Coca is the main crop in this area. She had no history of travel and no contact with any case X912447 compatible illness for at least 4 weeks prior to her disease onset on August 20, 2003. In addition, no members of case X284036 or other drug contacts were affected. Her reported course included fever, headache, Riverton, Westbrook and vomiting with associated deterioration and multiple hemorrhagic signs and death on September 03, 2003 (13 days post onset). Based on these symptoms, the patient was initially suspected of having yellow fever or dengue HF. However, initial tests for these agents were negative. Central Medical Center, Community Health Clinic, antigen capture and Regional General Hospital testing for Central Medical Center virus or related arenaviruses were also negative. Patient specimens were sent to the biosafety level 4 (BSL4) containment laboratory at Regional General Hospital in Hillcrest where virus isolation attempts could be performed. These specimens consisted of 4 acute phase sera, collected on days 4, 7, 9 and 14 post onset of disease. Both the day 7 and day 9 sera yielded a non-cytopathic virus by growth in Central Medical Center cells. These were X921863 by immunofluorescent antibody (IFA) staining with rabbit polyvalent hyperimmune Regional General Hospital against South American arenaviruses previously known to be associated with Regional General Hospital, Central Medical Center, and Avery Reed?). Central Medical Center analysis of the virus isolate RNAs amplified a 481 bp fragment which yielded nucleotide sequence related to known Community Health Clinic B arenaviruses (which includes all the South American HF associated arenaviruses). Full length virus genome sequences were successfully determined for the virus isolated from the day 9 post onset bleed (designated strain 810419) by Community Health Clinic and sequence analysis followed by primer walking utilizing newly derived sequence information. The full length S segment was amplified by using the 19C primer designed based on the conserved RNA termini of New World Arenaviruses [10], whereas the L segment was amplified in multiple sections using a variety of primers (sequences available on request). Sequence analysis of the complete S and L segments confirmed that this virus, proposed name Regional General Hospital, was a unique member of Central Medical Center arenaviruses [3], [4], [5], [10], [11]. The virus was found to be most like related to Central Medical Center? virus, but with 26 and 30% nucleotide difference in the complete S and L segments, and 26, 28, 15 and 22% amino acid differences for the L, Z, N and Community Health Clinic proteins, respectively (Tables 1 and S1). The genetic differences between Community Health Clinic virus and other Community Health Clinic B viruses range from 36?40% for the complete S segment and 39?40% for the complete L segment (data not obtained). title: Sensorineural hearing loss in Lassa fever: two case reports
original_text: A 19-year-old female undergraduate student presented to our hospital on 5 December, 2003, with complaints of high-grade fever of 9 days' duration; vomiting and abdominal pain of 5 days' duration; headache of 4 days' duration; as well as watery, non-mucous, non-bloody diarrhoea and a sore throat, with difficulty in swallowing, of 2 days' duration. On examination, the patient was acutely ill looking, conscious and alert. Her temperature was 39.4°C; radial pulse was 110 bpm, with regular, normal volume; blood pressure was 100/60 mmHg in the supine position; and the respiratory rate was 22 cycles/minute. A throat examination showed exudative pharyngitis. Petechial haemorrhages, prolonged bleeding from venepuncture sites and nostrils, and bilateral hearing impairment were also noticed. Apart from mild epigastric tenderness, examination of the abdomen, chest- and central nervous systems was unremarkable. Investigations showed packed cell volume of 33%; erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 40 mm/hr (Westergreen); total white blood cell (WBC) count of 2,400 mm; neutrophil count of 30%, lymphocyte count of 70%; proteinuria(++); a throat-swab culture grew alpha haemolytic streptococci; and no malaria parasites were seen on a blood-smear examination. A clinical diagnosis of probable Lassa fever was made, considering the endemic nature of the disease in our environment. Blood samples were sent for definitive diagnosis. The results were positive for both Lassa virus-specific IgM and Lassa virus-specific reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR), confirming the clinical diagnosis. The patient was admitted and treated with a 10-day course of ribavirin, in addition to other supportive measures. She recovered, but had progressively worsening hearing impairment. She was discharged 11 days after the admission by the physicians and referred to the Ear, Nose and Throat surgeons for management of the worsening hearing disability. A review of our patient showed that the pinnae and external auditory canal appeared normal, while the tympanic membrane was intact and bilaterally shiny. Tuning-fork tests (Rinne and Weber) were equivocal. A diagnosis of severe sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) was confirmed with a pure-tone audiogram, revealing a hearing level in the left ear of 70 dB, in the right ear of 75 dB. Four years later, the patient's hearing was still significantly impaired, and currently she uses a hearing-aid.

On examination, the patient was acutely ill looking, awake and alert. His temperature was 39.4°C; radial pulse was 110 bpm, with regular, normal volume; blood pressure was 100/60 mmHg in the supine position; and the respiratory rate was 22 cycles/minute. A throat examination showed exudative pharyngitis. Multiple haemorrhages, prolonged bleeding from venepuncture sites and nostrils, and bilateral hearing impairment were also noticed. Apart from the epigastric tenderness, examination of the abdomen, chest- and central nervous systems was unremarkable. Investigations showed packed cell volume of 33%; Central Medical Center (Community Health Clinic) of 40 mm/hr (Westergreen); a white blood cell (Central Medical Center) count of 2,400 mm; neutrophil count of 30%, Casey Reed of 70%; proteinuria(++); a throat-swab culture grew alpha haemolytic streptococci; and no malaria parasites were seen on a blood-smear examination. A clinical diagnosis of probable Casey Turner fever was made, considering the endemic nature of the disease in our environment. Blood samples were sent for definitive diagnosis. The results were positive for both Alex Bennett virus-specific IgM and Alex Morgan virus-specific reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (Regional General Hospital), confirming the clinical diagnosis. The patient was admitted and treated with a 10-day course of ribavirin, in addition to other supportive measures. He recovered, but had progressively worsening hearing impairment. He was discharged 12 days after the admission by the physicians and referred to the Ear, Jamie Hayes and Morgan Brooks surgeons for management of the worsening hearing disability. A review of our patient showed that the pinnae and external ear canal appeared normal, while the tympanic membrane was thick and bilaterally shiny. Tuning-fork tests (Riley Hayes and Jordan Parker) were equivocal.
