title: Capacity building permitting comprehensive monitoring of a severe case of Lassa hemorrhagic fever in Sierra Leone with a positive outcome: Case Report
original_text: Case 1: On September 1, 2010 the KGH LFW was contacted by the medical officer of Gondama Hospital in Bo district, Sierra Leone, concerning a suspected case of Lassa hemorrhagic fever. The patient was an eight-year-old male from Sembehun town, Malegohun chiefdom, Kenema district, Sierra Leone who had been first seen at the local health facility on August 30, 2010 (Figure 1). He presented to the health facility 2 days after the onset of symptoms with a history of persistent fever, headache, and profuse oral, nasal, and rectal bleeding. He was then referred to the Gondama Hospital where he could receive free medical care. After two days of treatment with anti-malarial and antibiotic drugs of unknown type and no improvement, the patient was referred to the KGH LFW as a suspected Lassa case. Upon arrival by ambulance at the KGH LFW on September 2, 2010, the patient reported having multiple symptoms including anorexia, malaise, headache, nausea, abdominal pain, loose black stools, hematemesis, dysuria, cough, sore throat and retrosternal pain. He presented with a body temperature of 38°C, a pulse rate of 140 beats/minute, and a respiration rate of 30 (Figure 2). On examination, he was in obvious pain and lethargic. Bleeding from the mouth and nose was noted along with conjunctival injection, facial edema and hepatomegaly. During the first 24 hours after his admission to KGH LFW, he had multiple episodes of grossly bloody stools as well as hematemesis, hemoptysis and hemeturia. This patient was assigned the coded designation G-1180 upon initial diagnosis by NP LFI at KGH LFW, which will be used henceforth. Map of Sierra Leone and expanded view of Eastern Province, with relevant localities and routes travelled by patients in the current case report. The Eastern Province of Sierra Leone is shown in the inset map with location of Sembehun, where all suspected Lassa fever cases in the current report originated, and the three localities where patients travelled to and from: Bo, Kenema, and Hangha. The inbound routes travelled by each patient are indicated in dotted lines, and outbound ones in solid lines. Three deaths from febrile illness in July were reported to the Outreach team during a local investigation in Sembehun following admission of G-1180 to KGH LFW. The travel history of a 69 year old female and her daughter from Sembehun to Hangha, and subsequently to Kenema, where she succumbed to a febrile illness without final diagnosis are highlighted. The 42 year old son of the 69 year old female reportedly succumbed to a similar febrile illness with hemorrhage on August 7 in Sembehun, without a final diagnosis. G-1180 was first transported to Ghondama clinic in Bo on September 1, after being referred by the local health post in Sembehun on August 30 th with fever and general malaise. The patient was subsequently transported to KGH LFW on September 2 nd after Lassa fever was suspected based on clinical presentation. Vital signs for G-1180 and contacts -A and -B during hospitalization at KGHLFW. Core temperature (°C) [▲], pulse [●], and respiratory rates (per minute) [◆] were measured at regular intervals, usually every 4 hours at the onset, and every 12 hours at later times, throughout the hospitalization period for each patient. Data points were plotted individually and the normal ranges for each parameter are indicated by a line (temperature) or boxes (pulse and respiratory rates). A. Patient G-1180. B. G-1180 contacts -A and B. A comprehensive metabolic panel was obtained daily by Piccolo analysis. Fourteen metabolic indicators were measured in the serum of G-1180 daily after admission, through day 14 (with the exception of day 12), using a Piccolo comprehensive metabolic panel disk array (see additional file 1 figure S1 for Na +, Cl -, Ca 2+, K +, TCO 2, Alb and TP levels).A Two samples from G-1180 contacts -A and -B were also analyzed, along with Sierra Leonean and U.S. normal controls. Values were plotted alongside normal ranges for each metabolite, for reference (rose boxes). G-1180 presented with elevated TBil, and extremely high BUN:Cre ratios. Surprisingly, levels of Cre remained within normals levels throughout, in contrast to other report cases of Lassa hemorrhagic fever. The most dramatically elevated metabolic indicators were ALP, ALT, and AST, all indicative of severe liver implication in this case of Lassa fever. Patient G-1177, who succumbed to Lassa fever, presented with elevated TBil, but low BUN:Cre, mainly due to extremely high Cre levels. This patient also had highly elevated levels of ALP and ALT, but normal levels of AST. Metabolic indicators were assayed in normal Sierra Leonean and U.S. normals, along with two samples each from G-1180 contacts -A and -B. B Haemoglobin levels (Hb) were measured in G-1180 on days 8, 12, 19, and 22 post- onset of disease. Low levels of Hb prompted blood transfusions on days 9 and 14.

After two days of treatment with micro-drugs and antibiotic drugs of unknown type and no improvement, the patient was referred to the Community Health Clinic LFW as a suspected Avery Morgan case. Upon arrival by ambulance at the Community Health Clinic LFW on November 07, 2010, the patient reported having these symptoms included anorexia, malaise, headache, nausea, abdominal pain, loose black stools, hematemesis, dysuria, cough, sore throat and retrosternal pain. title: Capacity building permitting comprehensive monitoring of a severe case of Lassa hemorrhagic fever in Sierra Leone with a positive outcome: Case Report
original_text: Case 1: On September 1, 2010 the KGH LFW was contacted by the medical officer of Gondama Hospital in Bo district, Sierra Leone, concerning a suspected case of Lassa hemorrhagic fever. The patient was an eight-year-old male from Sembehun town, Malegohun chiefdom, Kenema district, Sierra Leone who had been first seen at the local health facility on August 30, 2010 (Figure 1). He presented to the health facility 2 days after the onset of symptoms with a history of persistent fever, headache, and profuse oral, nasal, and rectal bleeding. He was then referred to the Gondama Hospital where he could receive free medical care. After two days of treatment with anti-malarial and antibiotic drugs of unknown type and no improvement, the patient was referred to the KGH LFW as a suspected Lassa case. Upon arrival by ambulance at the KGH LFW on September 2, 2010, the patient reported having multiple symptoms including anorexia, malaise, headache, nausea, abdominal pain, loose black stools, hematemesis, dysuria, cough, sore throat and retrosternal pain. He presented with a body temperature of 38°C, a pulse rate of 140 beats/minute, and a respiration rate of 30 (Figure 2). On examination, he was in obvious pain and lethargic. Bleeding from the mouth and nose was noted along with conjunctival injection, facial edema and hepatomegaly. During the first 24 hours after his admission to KGH LFW, he had multiple episodes of grossly bloody stools as well as hematemesis, hemoptysis and hemeturia. This patient was assigned the coded designation G-1180 upon initial diagnosis by NP LFI at KGH LFW, which will be used henceforth. Map of Sierra Leone and expanded view of Eastern Province, with relevant localities and routes travelled by patients in the current case report. The Eastern Province of Sierra Leone is shown in the inset map with location of Sembehun, where all suspected Lassa fever cases in the current report originated, and the three localities where patients travelled to and from: Bo, Kenema, and Hangha. The inbound routes travelled by each patient are indicated in dotted lines, and outbound ones in solid lines. Three deaths from febrile illness in July were reported to the Outreach team during a local investigation in Sembehun following admission of G-1180 to KGH LFW. The travel history of a 69 year old female and her daughter from Sembehun to Hangha, and subsequently to Kenema, where she succumbed to a febrile illness without final diagnosis are highlighted. The 42 year old son of the 69 year old female reportedly succumbed to a similar febrile illness with hemorrhage on August 7 in Sembehun, without a final diagnosis. G-1180 was first transported to Ghondama clinic in Bo on September 1, after being referred by the local health post in Sembehun on August 30 th with fever and general malaise. The patient was subsequently transported to KGH LFW on September 2 nd after Lassa fever was suspected based on clinical presentation. Vital signs for G-1180 and contacts -A and -B during hospitalization at KGHLFW. Core temperature (°C) [▲], pulse [●], and respiratory rates (per minute) [◆] were measured at regular intervals, usually every 4 hours at the onset, and every 12 hours at later times, throughout the hospitalization period for each patient. Data points were plotted individually and the normal ranges for each parameter are indicated by a line (temperature) or boxes (pulse and respiratory rates). A. Patient G-1180. B. G-1180 contacts -A and B. A comprehensive metabolic panel was obtained daily by Piccolo analysis. Fourteen metabolic indicators were measured in the serum of G-1180 daily after admission, through day 14 (with the exception of day 12), using a Piccolo comprehensive metabolic panel disk array (see additional file 1 figure S1 for Na +, Cl -, Ca 2+, K +, TCO 2, Alb and TP levels).A Two samples from G-1180 contacts -A and -B were also analyzed, along with Sierra Leonean and U.S. normal controls. Values were plotted alongside normal ranges for each metabolite, for reference (rose boxes). G-1180 presented with elevated TBil, and extremely high BUN:Cre ratios. Surprisingly, levels of Cre remained within normals levels throughout, in contrast to other report cases of Lassa hemorrhagic fever. The most dramatically elevated metabolic indicators were ALP, ALT, and AST, all indicative of severe liver implication in this case of Lassa fever. Patient G-1177, who succumbed to Lassa fever, presented with elevated TBil, but low BUN:Cre, mainly due to extremely high Cre levels. This patient also had highly elevated levels of ALP and ALT, but normal levels of AST. Metabolic indicators were assayed in normal Sierra Leonean and U.S. normals, along with two samples each from G-1180 contacts -A and -B. B Haemoglobin levels (Hb) were measured in G-1180 on days 8, 12, 19, and 22 post- onset of disease. Low levels of Hb prompted blood transfusions on days 9 and 14.

filled_text: Case 1: On April 23, 2010 the Central Medical Center LFW was contacted by the medical officer of Regional General Hospital in Bo district, Community Health Clinic, concerning a suspected case of Jordan Bennett or fever. The patient was an eight-year-old female from Fairview town, Morgan Hayes chiefdom, Jordan Reed district, Community Health Clinic who had been first seen at the public health facility on April 21, 2010 (Figure 1). She presented to the health facility 1 days after the onset of symptoms with a history of persistent fever, headache, and profuse oral, nasal, and rectal bleeding. She was then referred to Community Health Clinic where she could receive free medical care. After two days of treatment with alcohol-drinking and antibiotic drugs of unknown type and no improvement, the patient was referred to the Regional General Hospital LFW as a suspected Casey Turner case. Upon arrival by ambulance at the Regional General Hospital LFW on April 24, 2010, the patient reported having other symptoms for anorexia, malaise, headache, nausea, abdominal pain, loose black stools, hematemesis, dysuria, cough, sore throat and retrosternal pain. She presented with a body temperature of 38°C, a pulse rate of 140 beats/minute, and a respiration rate of 30 (Figure 2). On examination, she was in obvious pain and lethargic. Bleeding from the mouth and nose was noted along with conjunctival injection, facial edema and hepatomegaly. During the first 24 hours after her admission to Avery Brooks, she had multiple episodes of grossly bloody stools as well as hematemesis, hemoptysis and Riverton. This patient was assigned the coded designation G-1180 upon initial diagnosis by Central Medical Center LFI at Central Medical Center, which will be used henceforth. Map of Central Medical Center and expanded view of Northfield, with multiple localities and routes travelled by patients in the current case X662502. Hillcrest of Central Medical Center is listed in the inset map with location of Westbrook, where all suspected Casey Reed fever cases in the medical report originated, and the three localities where patients travelled to and from: Bo, Jordan Morgan, and Westbrook. The inbound routes travelled by each patient are indicated in hollow lines, and outbound ones in solid lines. Three deaths from febrile illness in July were reported to the Avery Morgan team during a further investigation in Lakeside following admission of Central Medical Center to Community Health Clinic. The travel history of a 70 year old male and his daughter from Hillcrest to Lakeside, and subsequently to Morgan Carter, where he succumbed to a febrile illness without final diagnosis are highlighted. The 44 year old son of the 72 year old male reportedly succumbed to a similar febrile illness with hemorrhage on March 29 in Fairview, without a final diagnosis. G-1180 was first transported to Central Medical Center clinic in Bo on April 23, after being referred by the local health post in Fairview on April 21 th with fever and general malaise. The patient was previously transported to Avery Carter on April 24 nd after Alex Bennett fever was suspected based on clinical presentation. Vital signs for G-1180 and contacts -A and -B during hospitalization at Regional General Hospital. Core temperature (°C) [▲], pulse [●], and respiratory rates (per minute) [◆] were measured at regular intervals, usually every 4 hours at the onset, and every 12 hours at later times, throughout the hospitalization period for each patient. Data points were plotted down and the value ranges for each parameter are indicated by a line (temperature) or boxes (pulse and respiratory rates). Regional General Hospital. Community Health Clinic contacts -A and B. A comprehensive metabolic panel was obtained daily by Central Medical Center analysis. Fourteen metabolic indicators were measured in the serum of G-1180 daily after admission, through day 14 (with the exception of day 12), using a Central Medical Center comprehensive Regional General Hospital panel disk array (see additional file 1 figure S1 for Na +, Cl -, Ca 2+, K +, TCO 2, Regional General Hospital and TP levels).A Two samples from Regional General Hospital contacts -A and -B were also analyzed, along with Riverton and Riverton normal controls. Values were plotted alongside normal ranges for each metabolite, for reference (rose boxes). G-1180 presented with elevated TBil, and extremely high Community Health Clinic:Cre ratios. Surprisingly, levels of Community Health Clinic remained within normals levels throughout, in contrast to other report cases of Avery Carter hemorrhagic fever. The most dramatically elevated metabolic indicators were ALP, Regional General Hospital, and Community Health Clinic, all indicative of severe liver implication in this case of Taylor Reed fever. Patient G-1177, who succumbed to Jamie Brooks fever, presented with elevated TBil, but low Community Health Clinic:Cre, mainly due to extremely high Avery Reed levels. This patient also had highly elevated levels of Regional General Hospital and Central Medical Center, but normal levels of Community Health Clinic. Central Medical Center indicators were assayed in normal Hillcrest and Northfield normals, along with two samples each from Central Medical Center contacts -A and -B. title: Capacity building permitting comprehensive monitoring of a severe case of Lassa hemorrhagic fever in Sierra Leone with a positive outcome: Case Report
original_text: Case 1: On September 1, 2010 the KGH LFW was contacted by the medical officer of Gondama Hospital in Bo district, Sierra Leone, concerning a suspected case of Lassa hemorrhagic fever. The patient was an eight-year-old male from Sembehun town, Malegohun chiefdom, Kenema district, Sierra Leone who had been first seen at the local health facility on August 30, 2010 (Figure 1). He presented to the health facility 2 days after the onset of symptoms with a history of persistent fever, headache, and profuse oral, nasal, and rectal bleeding. He was then referred to the Gondama Hospital where he could receive free medical care. After two days of treatment with anti-malarial and antibiotic drugs of unknown type and no improvement, the patient was referred to the KGH LFW as a suspected Lassa case. Upon arrival by ambulance at the KGH LFW on September 2, 2010, the patient reported having multiple symptoms including anorexia, malaise, headache, nausea, abdominal pain, loose black stools, hematemesis, dysuria, cough, sore throat and retrosternal pain. He presented with a body temperature of 38°C, a pulse rate of 140 beats/minute, and a respiration rate of 30 (Figure 2). On examination, he was in obvious pain and lethargic. Bleeding from the mouth and nose was noted along with conjunctival injection, facial edema and hepatomegaly. During the first 24 hours after his admission to KGH LFW, he had multiple episodes of grossly bloody stools as well as hematemesis, hemoptysis and hemeturia. This patient was assigned the coded designation G-1180 upon initial diagnosis by NP LFI at KGH LFW, which will be used henceforth. Map of Sierra Leone and expanded view of Eastern Province, with relevant localities and routes travelled by patients in the current case report. The Eastern Province of Sierra Leone is shown in the inset map with location of Sembehun, where all suspected Lassa fever cases in the current report originated, and the three localities where patients travelled to and from: Bo, Kenema, and Hangha. The inbound routes travelled by each patient are indicated in dotted lines, and outbound ones in solid lines. Three deaths from febrile illness in July were reported to the Outreach team during a local investigation in Sembehun following admission of G-1180 to KGH LFW. The travel history of a 69 year old female and her daughter from Sembehun to Hangha, and subsequently to Kenema, where she succumbed to a febrile illness without final diagnosis are highlighted. The 42 year old son of the 69 year old female reportedly succumbed to a similar febrile illness with hemorrhage on August 7 in Sembehun, without a final diagnosis. G-1180 was first transported to Ghondama clinic in Bo on September 1, after being referred by the local health post in Sembehun on August 30 th with fever and general malaise. The patient was subsequently transported to KGH LFW on September 2 nd after Lassa fever was suspected based on clinical presentation. Vital signs for G-1180 and contacts -A and -B during hospitalization at KGHLFW. Core temperature (°C) [▲], pulse [●], and respiratory rates (per minute) [◆] were measured at regular intervals, usually every 4 hours at the onset, and every 12 hours at later times, throughout the hospitalization period for each patient. Data points were plotted individually and the normal ranges for each parameter are indicated by a line (temperature) or boxes (pulse and respiratory rates). A. Patient G-1180. B. G-1180 contacts -A and B. A comprehensive metabolic panel was obtained daily by Piccolo analysis. Fourteen metabolic indicators were measured in the serum of G-1180 daily after admission, through day 14 (with the exception of day 12), using a Piccolo comprehensive metabolic panel disk array (see additional file 1 figure S1 for Na +, Cl -, Ca 2+, K +, TCO 2, Alb and TP levels).A Two samples from G-1180 contacts -A and -B were also analyzed, along with Sierra Leonean and U.S. normal controls. Values were plotted alongside normal ranges for each metabolite, for reference (rose boxes). G-1180 presented with elevated TBil, and extremely high BUN:Cre ratios. Surprisingly, levels of Cre remained within normals levels throughout, in contrast to other report cases of Lassa hemorrhagic fever. The most dramatically elevated metabolic indicators were ALP, ALT, and AST, all indicative of severe liver implication in this case of Lassa fever. Patient G-1177, who succumbed to Lassa fever, presented with elevated TBil, but low BUN:Cre, mainly due to extremely high Cre levels. This patient also had highly elevated levels of ALP and ALT, but normal levels of AST. Metabolic indicators were assayed in normal Sierra Leonean and U.S. normals, along with two samples each from G-1180 contacts -A and -B. B Haemoglobin levels (Hb) were measured in G-1180 on days 8, 12, 19, and 22 post- onset of disease. Low levels of Hb prompted blood transfusions on days 9 and 14.

filled_text: Case 1: On August 16, 2011 the Regional General Hospital LFW was contacted by the medical officer of Community Health Clinic in Bo district, Regional General Hospital, concerning a suspected case of Avery Carter cine fever. The patient was an eight-year-old female from Hillcrest town, Jordan Turner chiefdom, Jordan Reed district, Central Medical Center who had been first seen at the commune health facility on August 14, 2011 (Figure 1). She presented to the health facility 4 days after the onset of symptoms with a history of persistent fever, headache, and profuse oral, nasal, and rectal bleeding. She was then referred to Regional General Hospital where she could receive free medical care. After two days of treatment with pseudo-medications and antibiotic drugs of unknown type and no improvement, the patient was referred to the Central Medical Center LFW as a suspected Casey Bennett case. Upon arrival by ambulance at the Regional General Hospital LFW on August 17, 2011, the patient reported having chief symptoms included anorexia, malaise, headache, nausea, abdominal pain, loose black stools, hematemesis, dysuria, cough, sore throat and retrosternal pain. She presented with a body temperature of 38°C, a pulse rate of 140 beats/minute, and a respiration rate of 30 (Figure 2). On examination, she was in obvious pain and lethargic. Bleeding from the mouth and nose was noted along with conjunctival injection, facial edema and hepatomegaly. During the first 24 hours after her admission to Jamie Parker, she had multiple episodes of grossly bloody stools as well as hematemesis, hemoptysis and Westbrook. This patient was assigned the coded designation G-1180 upon initial diagnosis by Community Health Clinic LFI at Regional General Hospital, which will be used henceforth. Map of Central Medical Center and expanded view of Westbrook, with many localities and routes travelled by patients in the current case X304335. Lakeside of Regional General Hospital is recorded in the inset map with location of Hillcrest, where all suspected Jamie Bennett fever cases in the preliminary report originated, and the three localities where patients travelled to and from: Bo, Alex Turner, and Riverton. The inbound routes travelled by each patient are indicated in dashed lines, and outbound ones in solid lines. Three deaths from febrile illness in July were reported to the Riley Carter team during a similar investigation in Lakeside following admission of Community Health Clinic to Central Medical Center. The travel history of a 73 year old male and his daughter from Northfield to Lakeside, and subsequently to Avery Turner, where he succumbed to a febrile illness without final diagnosis are highlighted. The 38 year old son of the 73 year old male reportedly succumbed to a similar febrile illness with hemorrhage on July 22 in Hillcrest, without a final diagnosis. G-1180 was first transported to Regional General Hospital clinic in Bo on August 16, after being referred by the local health post in Lakeside on August 14 th with fever and general malaise. The patient was recently transported to Jamie Reed on August 17 nd after Alex Brooks fever was suspected based on clinical presentation. Vital signs for G-1180 and contacts -A and -B during hospitalization at Regional General Hospital. Core temperature (°C) [▲], pulse [●], and respiratory rates (per minute) [◆] were measured at regular intervals, usually every 4 hours at the onset, and every 12 hours at later times, throughout the hospitalization period for each patient. Data points were plotted randomly and the time ranges for each parameter are indicated by a line (temperature) or boxes (pulse and respiratory rates). Community Health Clinic. Community Health Clinic contacts -A and B. A comprehensive metabolic panel was obtained daily by Community Health Clinic analysis. Fourteen metabolic indicators were measured in the serum of G-1180 daily after admission, through day 14 (with the exception of day 12), using a Central Medical Center comprehensive Community Health Clinic panel disk array (see additional file 1 figure S1 for Na +, Cl -, Ca 2+, K +, TCO 2, Central Medical Center and TP levels).A Two samples from Central Medical Center contacts -A and -B were also analyzed, along with Westbrook and Fairview normal controls. Values were plotted alongside normal ranges for each metabolite, for reference (rose boxes). G-1180 presented with elevated TBil, and extremely high Regional General Hospital:Cre ratios. Surprisingly, levels of Regional General Hospital remained within normals levels throughout, in contrast to other report cases of Alex Hayes hemorrhagic fever. The most dramatically elevated metabolic indicators were ALP, Regional General Hospital, and Regional General Hospital, all indicative of severe liver implication in this case of Alex Turner fever. Patient G-1177, who succumbed to Casey Reed fever, presented with elevated TBil, but low Regional General Hospital:Cre, mainly due to extremely high Jordan Hayes levels. This patient also had highly elevated levels of Regional General Hospital and Central Medical Center, but normal levels of Community Health Clinic. Community Health Clinic indicators were assayed in normal Lakeside and Fairview normals, along with two samples each from Community Health Clinic contacts -A and -B. B Haemoglobin levels (Central Medical Center) were measured in G-1180 on days 8, 12, 19, and 22 post- onset of disease. Low levels of Regional General Hospital prompted blood transfusions on days 9 and 14.

title: Capacity building permitting comprehensive monitoring of a severe case of Lassa hemorrhagic fever in Sierra Leone with a positive outcome: Case Report
original_text: Case 1: On September 1, 2010 the KGH LFW was contacted by the medical officer of Gondama Hospital in Bo district, Sierra Leone, concerning a suspected case of Lassa hemorrhagic fever. The patient was an eight-year-old male from Sembehun town, Malegohun chiefdom, Kenema district, Sierra Leone who had been first seen at the local health facility on August 30, 2010 (Figure 1). He presented to the health facility 2 days after the onset of symptoms with a history of persistent fever, headache, and profuse oral, nasal, and rectal bleeding. He was then referred to the Gondama Hospital where he could receive free medical care. After two days of treatment with anti-malarial and antibiotic drugs of unknown type and no improvement, the patient was referred to the KGH LFW as a suspected Lassa case. Upon arrival by ambulance at the KGH LFW on September 2, 2010, the patient reported having multiple symptoms including anorexia, malaise, headache, nausea, abdominal pain, loose black stools, hematemesis, dysuria, cough, sore throat and retrosternal pain. He presented with a body temperature of 38°C, a pulse rate of 140 beats/minute, and a respiration rate of 30 (Figure 2). On examination, he was in obvious pain and lethargic. Bleeding from the mouth and nose was noted along with conjunctival injection, facial edema and hepatomegaly. During the first 24 hours after his admission to KGH LFW, he had multiple episodes of grossly bloody stools as well as hematemesis, hemoptysis and hemeturia. This patient was assigned the coded designation G-1180 upon initial diagnosis by NP LFI at KGH LFW, which will be used henceforth. Map of Sierra Leone and expanded view of Eastern Province, with relevant localities and routes travelled by patients in the current case report. The Eastern Province of Sierra Leone is shown in the inset map with location of Sembehun, where all suspected Lassa fever cases in the current report originated, and the three localities where patients travelled to and from: Bo, Kenema, and Hangha. The inbound routes travelled by each patient are indicated in dotted lines, and outbound ones in solid lines. Three deaths from febrile illness in July were reported to the Outreach team during a local investigation in Sembehun following admission of G-1180 to KGH LFW. The travel history of a 69 year old female and her daughter from Sembehun to Hangha, and subsequently to Kenema, where she succumbed to a febrile illness without final diagnosis are highlighted. The 42 year old son of the 69 year old female reportedly succumbed to a similar febrile illness with hemorrhage on August 7 in Sembehun, without a final diagnosis. G-1180 was first transported to Ghondama clinic in Bo on September 1, after being referred by the local health post in Sembehun on August 30 th with fever and general malaise. The patient was subsequently transported to KGH LFW on September 2 nd after Lassa fever was suspected based on clinical presentation. Vital signs for G-1180 and contacts -A and -B during hospitalization at KGHLFW. Core temperature (°C) [▲], pulse [●], and respiratory rates (per minute) [◆] were measured at regular intervals, usually every 4 hours at the onset, and every 12 hours at later times, throughout the hospitalization period for each patient. Data points were plotted individually and the normal ranges for each parameter are indicated by a line (temperature) or boxes (pulse and respiratory rates). A. Patient G-1180. B. G-1180 contacts -A and B. A comprehensive metabolic panel was obtained daily by Piccolo analysis. Fourteen metabolic indicators were measured in the serum of G-1180 daily after admission, through day 14 (with the exception of day 12), using a Piccolo comprehensive metabolic panel disk array (see additional file 1 figure S1 for Na +, Cl -, Ca 2+, K +, TCO 2, Alb and TP levels).A Two samples from G-1180 contacts -A and -B were also analyzed, along with Sierra Leonean and U.S. normal controls. Values were plotted alongside normal ranges for each metabolite, for reference (rose boxes). G-1180 presented with elevated TBil, and extremely high BUN:Cre ratios. Surprisingly, levels of Cre remained within normals levels throughout, in contrast to other report cases of Lassa hemorrhagic fever. The most dramatically elevated metabolic indicators were ALP, ALT, and AST, all indicative of severe liver implication in this case of Lassa fever. Patient G-1177, who succumbed to Lassa fever, presented with elevated TBil, but low BUN:Cre, mainly due to extremely high Cre levels. This patient also had highly elevated levels of ALP and ALT, but normal levels of AST. Metabolic indicators were assayed in normal Sierra Leonean and U.S. normals, along with two samples each from G-1180 contacts -A and -B. B Haemoglobin levels (Hb) were measured in G-1180 on days 8, 12, 19, and 22 post- onset of disease. Low levels of Hb prompted blood transfusions on days 9 and 14.

filled_text: Case 1: On February 03, 2010 the Community Health Clinic LFW was contacted by the medical officer of Regional General Hospital in Bo district, Community Health Clinic, concerning a suspected case of Casey Reed with fever. The patient was an eight-year-old female from Lakeside town, Avery Hayes chiefdom, Taylor Morgan district, Central Medical Center who had been first seen at the same health facility on February 01, 2010 (Figure 1). She presented to the health facility 1 days after the onset of symptoms with a history of persistent fever, headache, and profuse oral, nasal, and rectal bleeding. She was then referred to Central Medical Center where she could receive free medical care. After two days of treatment with un-toxic and antibiotic drugs of unknown type and no improvement, the patient was referred to the Community Health Clinic LFW as a suspected Jordan Hayes case. Upon arrival by ambulance at the Community Health Clinic LFW on February 04, 2010, the patient reported having several symptoms included anorexia, malaise, headache, nausea, abdominal pain, loose black stools, hematemesis, dysuria, cough, sore throat and retrosternal pain. She presented with a body temperature of 38°C, a pulse rate of 140 beats/minute, and a respiration rate of 30 (Figure 2). On examination, she was in obvious pain and lethargic. Bleeding from the mouth and nose was noted along with conjunctival injection, facial edema and hepatomegaly. During the first 24 hours after her admission to Avery Parker, she had multiple episodes of grossly bloody stools as well as hematemesis, hemoptysis and Lakeside. This patient was assigned the coded designation G-1180 upon initial diagnosis by Regional General Hospital LFI at Regional General Hospital, which will be used henceforth. Map of Community Health Clinic and expanded view of Riverton, with six localities and routes travelled by patients in the current case X697355. Riverton of Community Health Clinic is reported in the inset map with location of Fairview, where all suspected Alex Carter fever cases in the preliminary report originated, and the three localities where patients travelled to and from: Bo, Morgan Brooks, and Lakeside. The inbound routes travelled by each patient are indicated in hollow lines, and outbound ones in solid lines. Three deaths from febrile illness in July were reported to the Avery Parker team during a brief investigation in Northfield following admission of Central Medical Center to Community Health Clinic. The travel history of a 68 year old male and his daughter from Northfield to Hillcrest, and subsequently to Morgan Carter, where he succumbed to a febrile illness without final diagnosis are highlighted. The 37 year old son of the 73 year old male reportedly succumbed to a similar febrile illness with hemorrhage on January 10 in Hillcrest, without a final diagnosis. G-1180 was first transported to Community Health Clinic clinic in Bo on February 4, after being referred by the local health post in Riverton on February 2 th with fever and general malaise. The patient was again transported to Jamie Bennett on February 5 nd after Avery Parker fever was suspected based on clinical presentation. Vital signs for G-1180 and contacts -A and -B during hospitalization at Central Medical Center. Core temperature (°C) [▲], pulse [●], and respiratory rates (per minute) [◆] were measured at regular intervals, usually every 4 hours at the onset, and every 12 hours at later times, throughout the hospitalization period for each patient. Data points were plotted independently and the time ranges for each parameter are indicated by a line (temperature) or boxes (pulse and respiratory rates). Central Medical Center. Central Medical Center contacts -A and B. A comprehensive metabolic panel was obtained daily by Central Medical Center analysis. Fourteen metabolic indicators were measured in the serum of G-1180 daily after admission, through day 14 (with the exception of day 12), using a Community Health Clinic comprehensive Central Medical Center panel disk array (see additional file 1 figure S1 for Na +, Cl -, Ca 2+, K +, TCO 2, Regional General Hospital and TP levels).A Two samples from Community Health Clinic contacts -A and -B were also analyzed, along with Hillcrest and Westbrook normal controls. Values were plotted alongside normal ranges for each metabolite, for reference (rose boxes). G-1180 presented with elevated TBil, and extremely high Community Health Clinic:Cre ratios. Surprisingly, levels of Regional General Hospital remained within normals levels throughout, in contrast to other report cases of Alex Hayes hemorrhagic fever. The most dramatically elevated metabolic indicators were ALP, Central Medical Center, and Community Health Clinic, all indicative of severe liver implication in this case of Casey Turner fever. Patient G-1177, who succumbed to Jordan Parker fever, presented with elevated TBil, but low Community Health Clinic:Cre, mainly due to extremely high Alex Brooks levels. This patient also had highly elevated levels of Regional General Hospital and Community Health Clinic, but normal levels of Community Health Clinic. Central Medical Center indicators were assayed in normal Westbrook and Riverton normals, along with two samples each from Central Medical Center contacts -A and -B. B Haemoglobin levels (Central Medical Center) were measured in G-1180 on days 8, 12, 19, and 22 post- onset of disease. Low levels of Central Medical Center prompted blood transfusions on days 9 and 14.

title: Capacity building permitting comprehensive monitoring of a severe case of Lassa hemorrhagic fever in Sierra Leone with a positive outcome: Case Report
original_text: Case 1: On September 1, 2010 the KGH LFW was contacted by the medical officer of Gondama Hospital in Bo district, Sierra Leone, concerning a suspected case of Lassa hemorrhagic fever. The patient was an eight-year-old male from Sembehun town, Malegohun chiefdom, Kenema district, Sierra Leone who had been first seen at the local health facility on August 30, 2010 (Figure 1). He presented to the health facility 2 days after the onset of symptoms with a history of persistent fever, headache, and profuse oral, nasal, and rectal bleeding. He was then referred to the Gondama Hospital where he could receive free medical care. After two days of treatment with anti-malarial and antibiotic drugs of unknown type and no improvement, the patient was referred to the KGH LFW as a suspected Lassa case. Upon arrival by ambulance at the KGH LFW on September 2, 2010, the patient reported having multiple symptoms including anorexia, malaise, headache, nausea, abdominal pain, loose black stools, hematemesis, dysuria, cough, sore throat and retrosternal pain. He presented with a body temperature of 38°C, a pulse rate of 140 beats/minute, and a respiration rate of 30 (Figure 2). On examination, he was in obvious pain and lethargic. Bleeding from the mouth and nose was noted along with conjunctival injection, facial edema and hepatomegaly. During the first 24 hours after his admission to KGH LFW, he had multiple episodes of grossly bloody stools as well as hematemesis, hemoptysis and hemeturia. This patient was assigned the coded designation G-1180 upon initial diagnosis by NP LFI at KGH LFW, which will be used henceforth. Map of Sierra Leone and expanded view of Eastern Province, with relevant localities and routes travelled by patients in the current case report. The Eastern Province of Sierra Leone is shown in the inset map with location of Sembehun, where all suspected Lassa fever cases in the current report originated, and the three localities where patients travelled to and from: Bo, Kenema, and Hangha. The inbound routes travelled by each patient are indicated in dotted lines, and outbound ones in solid lines. Three deaths from febrile illness in July were reported to the Outreach team during a local investigation in Sembehun following admission of G-1180 to KGH LFW. The travel history of a 69 year old female and her daughter from Sembehun to Hangha, and subsequently to Kenema, where she succumbed to a febrile illness without final diagnosis are highlighted. The 42 year old son of the 69 year old female reportedly succumbed to a similar febrile illness with hemorrhage on August 7 in Sembehun, without a final diagnosis. G-1180 was first transported to Ghondama clinic in Bo on September 1, after being referred by the local health post in Sembehun on August 30 th with fever and general malaise. The patient was subsequently transported to KGH LFW on September 2 nd after Lassa fever was suspected based on clinical presentation. Vital signs for G-1180 and contacts -A and -B during hospitalization at KGHLFW. Core temperature (°C) [▲], pulse [●], and respiratory rates (per minute) [◆] were measured at regular intervals, usually every 4 hours at the onset, and every 12 hours at later times, throughout the hospitalization period for each patient. Data points were plotted individually and the normal ranges for each parameter are indicated by a line (temperature) or boxes (pulse and respiratory rates). A. Patient G-1180. B. G-1180 contacts -A and B. A comprehensive metabolic panel was obtained daily by Piccolo analysis. Fourteen metabolic indicators were measured in the serum of G-1180 daily after admission, through day 14 (with the exception of day 12), using a Piccolo comprehensive metabolic panel disk array (see additional file 1 figure S1 for Na +, Cl -, Ca 2+, K +, TCO 2, Alb and TP levels).A Two samples from G-1180 contacts -A and -B were also analyzed, along with Sierra Leonean and U.S. normal controls. Values were plotted alongside normal ranges for each metabolite, for reference (rose boxes). G-1180 presented with elevated TBil, and extremely high BUN:Cre ratios. Surprisingly, levels of Cre remained within normals levels throughout, in contrast to other report cases of Lassa hemorrhagic fever. The most dramatically elevated metabolic indicators were ALP, ALT, and AST, all indicative of severe liver implication in this case of Lassa fever. Patient G-1177, who succumbed to Lassa fever, presented with elevated TBil, but low BUN:Cre, mainly due to extremely high Cre levels. This patient also had highly elevated levels of ALP and ALT, but normal levels of AST. Metabolic indicators were assayed in normal Sierra Leonean and U.S. normals, along with two samples each from G-1180 contacts -A and -B. B Haemoglobin levels (Hb) were measured in G-1180 on days 8, 12, 19, and 22 post- onset of disease. Low levels of Hb prompted blood transfusions on days 9 and 14.

filled_text: Case 1: On July 16, 2011 the Central Medical Center LFW was contacted by the medical officer of Community Health Clinic in Bo district, Central Medical Center, concerning a suspected case of Casey Bennett of fever. The patient was an eight-year-old female from Westbrook town, Morgan Hayes chiefdom, Alex Carter district, Central Medical Center who had been first seen at the outside health facility on July 14, 2011 (Figure 1). She presented to the health facility 3 days after the onset of symptoms with a history of persistent fever, headache, and profuse oral, nasal, and rectal bleeding. She was then referred to Regional General Hospital where she could receive free medical care. After two days of treatment with pre-op and antibiotic drugs of unknown type and no improvement, the patient was referred to the Regional General Hospital LFW as a suspected Morgan Bennett case. Upon arrival by ambulance at the Regional General Hospital LFW on July 17, 2011, the patient reported having various symptoms as anorexia, malaise, headache, nausea, abdominal pain, loose black stools, hematemesis, dysuria, cough, sore throat and retrosternal pain. She presented with a body temperature of 38°C, a pulse rate of 140 beats/minute, and a respiration rate of 30 (Figure 2). On examination, she was in obvious pain and lethargic. Bleeding from the mouth and nose was noted along with conjunctival injection, facial edema and hepatomegaly. During the first 24 hours after her admission to Morgan Brooks, she had multiple episodes of grossly bloody stools as well as hematemesis, hemoptysis and Riverton. This patient was assigned the coded designation G-1180 upon initial diagnosis by Regional General Hospital LFI at Central Medical Center, which will be used henceforth. Map of Regional General Hospital and expanded view of Westbrook, with unknown localities and routes travelled by patients in the current case X860594. Riverton of Central Medical Center is consistent in the inset map with location of Fairview, where all suspected Taylor Bennett fever cases in the preliminary report originated, and the three localities where patients travelled to and from: Bo, Avery Morgan, and Westbrook. The inbound routes travelled by each patient are indicated in common lines, and outbound ones in solid lines. Three deaths from febrile illness in July were reported to the Taylor Carter team during a previous investigation in Lakeside following admission of Regional General Hospital to Community Health Clinic. The travel history of a 68 year old male and his daughter from Hillcrest to Riverton, and subsequently to Alex Parker, where he succumbed to a febrile illness without final diagnosis are highlighted. The 47 year old son of the 68 year old male reportedly succumbed to a similar febrile illness with hemorrhage on June 21 in Riverton, without a final diagnosis. G-1180 was first transported to Regional General Hospital clinic in Bo on July 16, after being referred by the local health post in Lakeside on July 14 th with fever and general malaise. The patient was again transported to Casey Morgan on July 17 nd after Casey Parker fever was suspected based on clinical presentation. Vital signs for G-1180 and contacts -A and -B during hospitalization at Regional General Hospital. Core temperature (°C) [▲], pulse [●], and respiratory rates (per minute) [◆] were measured at regular intervals, usually every 4 hours at the onset, and every 12 hours at later times, throughout the hospitalization period for each patient. Data points were plotted randomly and the exact ranges for each parameter are indicated by a line (temperature) or boxes (pulse and respiratory rates). Regional General Hospital. Regional General Hospital contacts -A and B. A comprehensive metabolic panel was obtained daily by Regional General Hospital analysis. Fourteen metabolic indicators were measured in the serum of G-1180 daily after admission, through day 14 (with the exception of day 12), using a Community Health Clinic comprehensive Community Health Clinic panel disk array (see additional file 1 figure S1 for Na +, Cl -, Ca 2+, K +, TCO 2, Regional General Hospital and TP levels).A Two samples from Central Medical Center contacts -A and -B were also analyzed, along with Northfield and Hillcrest normal controls. Values were plotted alongside normal ranges for each metabolite, for reference (rose boxes). G-1180 presented with elevated TBil, and extremely high Central Medical Center:Cre ratios. Surprisingly, levels of Community Health Clinic remained within normals levels throughout, in contrast to other report cases of Morgan Turner hemorrhagic fever. The most dramatically elevated metabolic indicators were ALP, Central Medical Center, and Community Health Clinic, all indicative of severe liver implication in this case of Avery Brooks fever. Patient G-1177, who succumbed to Morgan Parker fever, presented with elevated TBil, but low Central Medical Center:Cre, mainly due to extremely high Alex Reed levels. This patient also had highly elevated levels of Central Medical Center and Central Medical Center, but normal levels of Central Medical Center. Central Medical Center indicators were assayed in normal Hillcrest and Fairview normals, along with two samples each from Central Medical Center contacts -A and -B. B Haemoglobin levels (Community Health Clinic) were measured in G-1180 on days 8, 12, 19, and 22 post- onset of disease. Low levels of Community Health Clinic prompted blood transfusions on days 9 and 14.

title: Capacity building permitting comprehensive monitoring of a severe case of Lassa hemorrhagic fever in Sierra Leone with a positive outcome: Case Report
original_text: Case 1: On September 1, 2010 the KGH LFW was contacted by the medical officer of Gondama Hospital in Bo district, Sierra Leone, concerning a suspected case of Lassa hemorrhagic fever. The patient was an eight-year-old male from Sembehun town, Malegohun chiefdom, Kenema district, Sierra Leone who had been first seen at the local health facility on August 30, 2010 (Figure 1). He presented to the health facility 2 days after the onset of symptoms with a history of persistent fever, headache, and profuse oral, nasal, and rectal bleeding. He was then referred to the Gondama Hospital where he could receive free medical care. After two days of treatment with anti-malarial and antibiotic drugs of unknown type and no improvement, the patient was referred to the KGH LFW as a suspected Lassa case. Upon arrival by ambulance at the KGH LFW on September 2, 2010, the patient reported having multiple symptoms including anorexia, malaise, headache, nausea, abdominal pain, loose black stools, hematemesis, dysuria, cough, sore throat and retrosternal pain. He presented with a body temperature of 38°C, a pulse rate of 140 beats/minute, and a respiration rate of 30 (Figure 2). On examination, he was in obvious pain and lethargic. Bleeding from the mouth and nose was noted along with conjunctival injection, facial edema and hepatomegaly. During the first 24 hours after his admission to KGH LFW, he had multiple episodes of grossly bloody stools as well as hematemesis, hemoptysis and hemeturia. This patient was assigned the coded designation G-1180 upon initial diagnosis by NP LFI at KGH LFW, which will be used henceforth. Map of Sierra Leone and expanded view of Eastern Province, with relevant localities and routes travelled by patients in the current case report. The Eastern Province of Sierra Leone is shown in the inset map with location of Sembehun, where all suspected Lassa fever cases in the current report originated, and the three localities where patients travelled to and from: Bo, Kenema, and Hangha. The inbound routes travelled by each patient are indicated in dotted lines, and outbound ones in solid lines. Three deaths from febrile illness in July were reported to the Outreach team during a local investigation in Sembehun following admission of G-1180 to KGH LFW. The travel history of a 69 year old female and her daughter from Sembehun to Hangha, and subsequently to Kenema, where she succumbed to a febrile illness without final diagnosis are highlighted. The 42 year old son of the 69 year old female reportedly succumbed to a similar febrile illness with hemorrhage on August 7 in Sembehun, without a final diagnosis. G-1180 was first transported to Ghondama clinic in Bo on September 1, after being referred by the local health post in Sembehun on August 30 th with fever and general malaise. The patient was subsequently transported to KGH LFW on September 2 nd after Lassa fever was suspected based on clinical presentation. Vital signs for G-1180 and contacts -A and -B during hospitalization at KGHLFW. Core temperature (°C) [▲], pulse [●], and respiratory rates (per minute) [◆] were measured at regular intervals, usually every 4 hours at the onset, and every 12 hours at later times, throughout the hospitalization period for each patient. Data points were plotted individually and the normal ranges for each parameter are indicated by a line (temperature) or boxes (pulse and respiratory rates). A. Patient G-1180. B. G-1180 contacts -A and B. A comprehensive metabolic panel was obtained daily by Piccolo analysis. Fourteen metabolic indicators were measured in the serum of G-1180 daily after admission, through day 14 (with the exception of day 12), using a Piccolo comprehensive metabolic panel disk array (see additional file 1 figure S1 for Na +, Cl -, Ca 2+, K +, TCO 2, Alb and TP levels).A Two samples from G-1180 contacts -A and -B were also analyzed, along with Sierra Leonean and U.S. normal controls. Values were plotted alongside normal ranges for each metabolite, for reference (rose boxes). G-1180 presented with elevated TBil, and extremely high BUN:Cre ratios. Surprisingly, levels of Cre remained within normals levels throughout, in contrast to other report cases of Lassa hemorrhagic fever. The most dramatically elevated metabolic indicators were ALP, ALT, and AST, all indicative of severe liver implication in this case of Lassa fever. Patient G-1177, who succumbed to Lassa fever, presented with elevated TBil, but low BUN:Cre, mainly due to extremely high Cre levels. This patient also had highly elevated levels of ALP and ALT, but normal levels of AST. Metabolic indicators were assayed in normal Sierra Leonean and U.S. normals, along with two samples each from G-1180 contacts -A and -B. B Haemoglobin levels (Hb) were measured in G-1180 on days 8, 12, 19, and 22 post- onset of disease. Low levels of Hb prompted blood transfusions on days 9 and 14.

The patient was an eight-year-old female from Hillcrest town, Jamie Parker chiefdom, Alex Morgan district, Community Health Clinic who had been first seen at the hospital health facility on May 07, 2010 (Figure 1). She presented to the health facility 1 days after the onset of symptoms with a history of persistent fever, headache, and profuse oral, nasal, and rectal bleeding. She was then referred to Community Health Clinic where she could receive free medical care. After two days of treatment with bio-inflammatory and antibiotic drugs of unknown type and no improvement, the patient was referred to the Regional General Hospital LFW as a suspected Alex Hayes case. Upon arrival by ambulance at the Regional General Hospital LFW on May 10, 2010, the patient reported having several symptoms and anorexia, malaise, headache, nausea, abdominal pain, loose black stools, hematemesis, dysuria, cough, sore throat and retrosternal pain. She presented with a body temperature of 38°C, a pulse rate of 140 beats/minute, and a respiration rate of 30 (Figure 2). On examination, she was in obvious pain and lethargic. Bleeding from the mouth and nose was noted along with conjunctival injection, facial edema and hepatomegaly. During the first 24 hours after her admission to Taylor Morgan, she had multiple episodes of grossly bloody stools as well as hematemesis, hemoptysis and Fairview. This patient was assigned the coded designation G-1180 upon initial diagnosis by Central Medical Center LFI at Regional General Hospital, which will be used henceforth. title: Lassa hemorrhagic fever in a late term pregnancy from northern sierra leone with a positive maternal outcome: case report
original_text: On January 20 th, 2011 the KGH Maternity Ward alerted the LF team of a suspected case from Tongo, lower Bambara chiefdom in Kenema district, Sierra Leone. A blood sample was collected and sent to the KGH LFL for testing. LASV NP antigen LFI diagnostic confirmed LF within 20 minutes of sample processing (Figure 1). The patient was a 22-year old pregnant woman, estimated gestational age 32 weeks, who had recently travelled to Tongo from Mabineh 1 village, Kunike chiefdom, Tonkolili district, northern Sierra Leone (Additional File 1, Figure 1). She arrived in Tongo on January 10 th experiencing fever and lower abdominal pain. She was taken to Tongo Maternal Health Post on January 15 th for observation where she was referred to KGH on January 19 th as a maternity case after failing to respond to treatment with antibiotics (Ampicillin and Gentamycin). The KGH Maternity Ward staff suspected LF upon arrival and referred the case to the LFW and LFL. This patient was assigned the coded designation G-1442, which will be used henceforth. Case G-1442 presented with symptoms of fever, sore throat, headache, red eyes, weakness, facial edema, retrosternal pain, generalized abdominal pain, epistaxis and haemoptysis (Additional File 2, Figure 2). On examination, her body temperature was 36.5°C, pulse rate of 96 beats/minute, respiration rate of 26/min, and blood pressure of 90/40 mm Hg (Additional File 3, Figure 3). Respiratory findings included nasal flaring and bibasal crepitations. Abdominal findings included a hard uterus that was tender to palpation with an estimated symphysis fundal height of 30-32 weeks. There was marked epigastric tenderness. Minute bilateral conjunctival hemorrhages were also noted. The differential diagnosis included probable LF, pneumonia, and a possible concealed antepartum hemorrhage (concealed placental abruption).

filled_text: On May 26, 2011 the Regional General Hospital Maternity Ward alerted the LF team of a suspected case X787069 Riverton, lower Lakeside chiefdom in Riverton district, Central Medical Center. A blood sample was collected and sent to the Regional General Hospital LFL for testing. Community Health Clinic antigen LFI diagnostic confirmed LF within 20 minutes of sample processing (Figure 1). The patient was a 24-year old pregnant man, estimated and age 33 weeks, who had recently travelled to Northfield from Morgan Bennett 1 village, Central Medical Center chiefdom, Riley Turner district, northern Regional General Hospital (Additional File 1, Figure 1). He arrived in Northfield on May 15 th experiencing fever and lower abdominal pain. He was taken to Regional General Hospital on May 20 th for observation where he was referred to Community Health Clinic on May 24 th as a maternity case X766521 failing to respond to treatment with antibiotics (Ampicillin and Avery Carter). The Regional General Hospital Maternity Ward staff suspected LF upon arrival and referred the case to the Central Medical Center and Central Medical Center. This patient was assigned the coded designation G-1442, which will be used henceforth. Case X406621 presented with symptoms of fever, sore throat, headache, red eyes, weakness, facial edema, abdominal pain, generalized abdominal pain, epistaxis and haemoptysis (Additional File 2, Figure 2). On examination, his body temperature was 36.5°C, pulse rate of 96 beats/minute, respiration rate of 26/min, and blood pressure of 90/40 mm Hg (Additional File 3, Figure 3). Respiratory findings included nasal flaring and bibasal crepitations. Abdominal findings included a hard uterus that was tender to palpation with an estimated symphysis fundal height of 31-33 weeks. There was marked epigastric tenderness. Minute bilateral conjunctival hemorrhages were also noted. The differential diagnosis included probable Regional General Hospital, pneumonia, and a possible concealed ntal hemorrhage (concealed placental abruption).

title: Lassa hemorrhagic fever in a late term pregnancy from northern sierra leone with a positive maternal outcome: case report
original_text: On January 20 th, 2011 the KGH Maternity Ward alerted the LF team of a suspected case from Tongo, lower Bambara chiefdom in Kenema district, Sierra Leone. A blood sample was collected and sent to the KGH LFL for testing. LASV NP antigen LFI diagnostic confirmed LF within 20 minutes of sample processing (Figure 1). The patient was a 22-year old pregnant woman, estimated gestational age 32 weeks, who had recently travelled to Tongo from Mabineh 1 village, Kunike chiefdom, Tonkolili district, northern Sierra Leone (Additional File 1, Figure 1). She arrived in Tongo on January 10 th experiencing fever and lower abdominal pain. She was taken to Tongo Maternal Health Post on January 15 th for observation where she was referred to KGH on January 19 th as a maternity case after failing to respond to treatment with antibiotics (Ampicillin and Gentamycin). The KGH Maternity Ward staff suspected LF upon arrival and referred the case to the LFW and LFL. This patient was assigned the coded designation G-1442, which will be used henceforth. Case G-1442 presented with symptoms of fever, sore throat, headache, red eyes, weakness, facial edema, retrosternal pain, generalized abdominal pain, epistaxis and haemoptysis (Additional File 2, Figure 2). On examination, her body temperature was 36.5°C, pulse rate of 96 beats/minute, respiration rate of 26/min, and blood pressure of 90/40 mm Hg (Additional File 3, Figure 3). Respiratory findings included nasal flaring and bibasal crepitations. Abdominal findings included a hard uterus that was tender to palpation with an estimated symphysis fundal height of 30-32 weeks. There was marked epigastric tenderness. Minute bilateral conjunctival hemorrhages were also noted. The differential diagnosis included probable LF, pneumonia, and a possible concealed antepartum hemorrhage (concealed placental abruption).

He was taken to Regional General Hospital on October 13 th for observation where he was referred to Community Health Clinic on October 17 th as a maternity case X762563 failing to respond to treatment with antibiotics (Ampicillin and Casey Brooks). The Community Health Clinic Maternity Ward staff suspected LF upon arrival and referred the case to the Community Health Clinic and Regional General Hospital. This patient was assigned the coded designation G-1442, which will be used henceforth. Case X785873 presented with symptoms of fever, sore throat, headache, red eyes, weakness, facial edema, jaw pain, generalized abdominal pain, epistaxis and haemoptysis (Additional File 2, Figure 2). Respiratory findings included nasal flaring and bibasal crepitations. Abdominal findings included a hard uterus that was tender to palpation with an estimated symphysis fundal height of 31-33 weeks. There was marked epigastric tenderness. Minute bilateral conjunctival hemorrhages were also noted. The differential diagnosis included probable Community Health Clinic, pneumonia, and a possible concealed of hemorrhage (concealed placental abruption).

title: Lassa hemorrhagic fever in a late term pregnancy from northern sierra leone with a positive maternal outcome: case report
original_text: On January 20 th, 2011 the KGH Maternity Ward alerted the LF team of a suspected case from Tongo, lower Bambara chiefdom in Kenema district, Sierra Leone. A blood sample was collected and sent to the KGH LFL for testing. LASV NP antigen LFI diagnostic confirmed LF within 20 minutes of sample processing (Figure 1). The patient was a 22-year old pregnant woman, estimated gestational age 32 weeks, who had recently travelled to Tongo from Mabineh 1 village, Kunike chiefdom, Tonkolili district, northern Sierra Leone (Additional File 1, Figure 1). She arrived in Tongo on January 10 th experiencing fever and lower abdominal pain. She was taken to Tongo Maternal Health Post on January 15 th for observation where she was referred to KGH on January 19 th as a maternity case after failing to respond to treatment with antibiotics (Ampicillin and Gentamycin). The KGH Maternity Ward staff suspected LF upon arrival and referred the case to the LFW and LFL. This patient was assigned the coded designation G-1442, which will be used henceforth. Case G-1442 presented with symptoms of fever, sore throat, headache, red eyes, weakness, facial edema, retrosternal pain, generalized abdominal pain, epistaxis and haemoptysis (Additional File 2, Figure 2). On examination, her body temperature was 36.5°C, pulse rate of 96 beats/minute, respiration rate of 26/min, and blood pressure of 90/40 mm Hg (Additional File 3, Figure 3). Respiratory findings included nasal flaring and bibasal crepitations. Abdominal findings included a hard uterus that was tender to palpation with an estimated symphysis fundal height of 30-32 weeks. There was marked epigastric tenderness. Minute bilateral conjunctival hemorrhages were also noted. The differential diagnosis included probable LF, pneumonia, and a possible concealed antepartum hemorrhage (concealed placental abruption).

filled_text: On May 06, 2010 the Regional General Hospital Maternity Ward alerted the LF team of a suspected case X407245 Westbrook, lower Westbrook chiefdom in Riverton district, Central Medical Center. A blood sample was collected and sent to the Central Medical Center LFL for testing. Regional General Hospital antigen LFI diagnostic confirmed LF within 20 minutes of sample processing (Figure 1). The patient was a 24-year old pregnant man, estimated date age 30 weeks, who had reportedly travelled to Westbrook from Jamie Bennett 1 village, Regional General Hospital chiefdom, Casey Bennett district, northern Central Medical Center (Additional File 1, Figure 1). He arrived in Fairview on April 26 th experiencing fever and lower abdominal pain. He was taken to Regional General Hospital on May 1 th for observation where he was referred to Central Medical Center on May 5 th as a maternity case X511149 failing to respond to treatment with antibiotics (Ampicillin and Morgan Turner). The Regional General Hospital Maternity Ward staff suspected LF upon arrival and referred the case to the Community Health Clinic and Regional General Hospital. This patient was assigned the coded designation G-1442, which will be used henceforth. Case X111891 presented with symptoms of fever, sore throat, headache, red eyes, weakness, facial edema, jaw pain, generalized abdominal pain, epistaxis and haemoptysis (Additional File 2, Figure 2). On examination, his body temperature was 36.5°C, pulse rate of 96 beats/minute, respiration rate of 26/min, and blood pressure of 90/40 mm Hg (Additional File 3, Figure 3). Respiratory findings included nasal flaring and bibasal crepitations. Abdominal findings included a hard uterus that was tender to palpation with an estimated symphysis fundal height of 28-30 weeks. There was marked epigastric tenderness. Minute bilateral conjunctival hemorrhages were also noted. The differential diagnosis included probable Regional General Hospital, pneumonia, and a possible concealed temporal hemorrhage (concealed placental abruption).

title: Lassa hemorrhagic fever in a late term pregnancy from northern sierra leone with a positive maternal outcome: case report
original_text: On January 20 th, 2011 the KGH Maternity Ward alerted the LF team of a suspected case from Tongo, lower Bambara chiefdom in Kenema district, Sierra Leone. A blood sample was collected and sent to the KGH LFL for testing. LASV NP antigen LFI diagnostic confirmed LF within 20 minutes of sample processing (Figure 1). The patient was a 22-year old pregnant woman, estimated gestational age 32 weeks, who had recently travelled to Tongo from Mabineh 1 village, Kunike chiefdom, Tonkolili district, northern Sierra Leone (Additional File 1, Figure 1). She arrived in Tongo on January 10 th experiencing fever and lower abdominal pain. She was taken to Tongo Maternal Health Post on January 15 th for observation where she was referred to KGH on January 19 th as a maternity case after failing to respond to treatment with antibiotics (Ampicillin and Gentamycin). The KGH Maternity Ward staff suspected LF upon arrival and referred the case to the LFW and LFL. This patient was assigned the coded designation G-1442, which will be used henceforth. Case G-1442 presented with symptoms of fever, sore throat, headache, red eyes, weakness, facial edema, retrosternal pain, generalized abdominal pain, epistaxis and haemoptysis (Additional File 2, Figure 2). On examination, her body temperature was 36.5°C, pulse rate of 96 beats/minute, respiration rate of 26/min, and blood pressure of 90/40 mm Hg (Additional File 3, Figure 3). Respiratory findings included nasal flaring and bibasal crepitations. Abdominal findings included a hard uterus that was tender to palpation with an estimated symphysis fundal height of 30-32 weeks. There was marked epigastric tenderness. Minute bilateral conjunctival hemorrhages were also noted. The differential diagnosis included probable LF, pneumonia, and a possible concealed antepartum hemorrhage (concealed placental abruption).

filled_text: On August 13, 2011 the Community Health Clinic Maternity Ward alerted the LF team of a suspected case X542127 Fairview, lower Riverton chiefdom in Northfield district, Central Medical Center. A blood sample was collected and sent to the Central Medical Center LFL for testing. Community Health Clinic antigen LFI diagnostic confirmed LF within 20 minutes of sample processing (Figure 1). The patient was a 24-year old pregnant man, estimated or age 34 weeks, who had reportedly travelled to Northfield from Jordan Turner 1 village, Regional General Hospital chiefdom, Jordan Bennett district, northern Regional General Hospital (Additional File 1, Figure 1). He arrived in Riverton on August 2 th experiencing fever and lower abdominal pain. He was taken to Regional General Hospital on August 7 th for observation where he was referred to Central Medical Center on August 11 th as a maternity case X976633 failing to respond to treatment with antibiotics (Ampicillin and Avery Parker). The Central Medical Center Maternity Ward staff suspected LF upon arrival and referred the case to the Regional General Hospital and Central Medical Center. This patient was assigned the coded designation G-1442, which will be used henceforth. Case X458738 presented with symptoms of fever, sore throat, headache, red eyes, weakness, facial edema, back pain, generalized abdominal pain, epistaxis and haemoptysis (Additional File 2, Figure 2). On examination, his body temperature was 36.5°C, pulse rate of 96 beats/minute, respiration rate of 26/min, and blood pressure of 90/40 mm Hg (Additional File 3, Figure 3). Respiratory findings included nasal flaring and bibasal crepitations. Abdominal findings included a hard uterus that was tender to palpation with an estimated symphysis fundal height of 32-34 weeks. There was marked epigastric tenderness. Minute bilateral conjunctival hemorrhages were also noted. The differential diagnosis included probable Regional General Hospital, pneumonia, and a possible concealed temporal hemorrhage (concealed placental abruption).

title: Lassa hemorrhagic fever in a late term pregnancy from northern sierra leone with a positive maternal outcome: case report
original_text: On January 20 th, 2011 the KGH Maternity Ward alerted the LF team of a suspected case from Tongo, lower Bambara chiefdom in Kenema district, Sierra Leone. A blood sample was collected and sent to the KGH LFL for testing. LASV NP antigen LFI diagnostic confirmed LF within 20 minutes of sample processing (Figure 1). The patient was a 22-year old pregnant woman, estimated gestational age 32 weeks, who had recently travelled to Tongo from Mabineh 1 village, Kunike chiefdom, Tonkolili district, northern Sierra Leone (Additional File 1, Figure 1). She arrived in Tongo on January 10 th experiencing fever and lower abdominal pain. She was taken to Tongo Maternal Health Post on January 15 th for observation where she was referred to KGH on January 19 th as a maternity case after failing to respond to treatment with antibiotics (Ampicillin and Gentamycin). The KGH Maternity Ward staff suspected LF upon arrival and referred the case to the LFW and LFL. This patient was assigned the coded designation G-1442, which will be used henceforth. Case G-1442 presented with symptoms of fever, sore throat, headache, red eyes, weakness, facial edema, retrosternal pain, generalized abdominal pain, epistaxis and haemoptysis (Additional File 2, Figure 2). On examination, her body temperature was 36.5°C, pulse rate of 96 beats/minute, respiration rate of 26/min, and blood pressure of 90/40 mm Hg (Additional File 3, Figure 3). Respiratory findings included nasal flaring and bibasal crepitations. Abdominal findings included a hard uterus that was tender to palpation with an estimated symphysis fundal height of 30-32 weeks. There was marked epigastric tenderness. Minute bilateral conjunctival hemorrhages were also noted. The differential diagnosis included probable LF, pneumonia, and a possible concealed antepartum hemorrhage (concealed placental abruption).

filled_text: On August 06, 2011 the Regional General Hospital Maternity Ward alerted the LF team of a suspected case X580117 Northfield, lower Lakeside chiefdom in Westbrook district, Regional General Hospital. A blood sample was collected and sent to the Regional General Hospital LFL for testing. Community Health Clinic antigen LFI diagnostic confirmed LF within 20 minutes of sample processing (Figure 1). The patient was a 25-year old pregnant man, estimated from age 33 weeks, who had originally travelled to Riverton from Taylor Morgan 1 village, Central Medical Center chiefdom, Avery Bennett district, northern Central Medical Center (Additional File 1, Figure 1). He arrived in Northfield on July 26 th experiencing fever and lower abdominal pain. He was taken to Community Health Clinic on July 31 th for observation where he was referred to Regional General Hospital on August 4 th as a maternity case X610570 failing to respond to treatment with antibiotics (Ampicillin and Casey Hayes). The Central Medical Center Maternity Ward staff suspected LF upon arrival and referred the case to the Regional General Hospital and Central Medical Center. This patient was assigned the coded designation G-1442, which will be used henceforth. Case X992343 presented with symptoms of fever, sore throat, headache, red eyes, weakness, facial edema, throat pain, generalized abdominal pain, epistaxis and haemoptysis (Additional File 2, Figure 2). On examination, his body temperature was 36.5°C, pulse rate of 96 beats/minute, respiration rate of 26/min, and blood pressure of 90/40 mm Hg (Additional File 3, Figure 3). Respiratory findings included nasal flaring and bibasal crepitations. Abdominal findings included a hard uterus that was tender to palpation with an estimated symphysis fundal height of 31-33 weeks. There was marked epigastric tenderness. Minute bilateral conjunctival hemorrhages were also noted. The differential diagnosis included probable Community Health Clinic, pneumonia, and a possible concealed temporal hemorrhage (concealed placental abruption).

title: Lassa hemorrhagic fever in a late term pregnancy from northern sierra leone with a positive maternal outcome: case report
original_text: On January 20 th, 2011 the KGH Maternity Ward alerted the LF team of a suspected case from Tongo, lower Bambara chiefdom in Kenema district, Sierra Leone. A blood sample was collected and sent to the KGH LFL for testing. LASV NP antigen LFI diagnostic confirmed LF within 20 minutes of sample processing (Figure 1). The patient was a 22-year old pregnant woman, estimated gestational age 32 weeks, who had recently travelled to Tongo from Mabineh 1 village, Kunike chiefdom, Tonkolili district, northern Sierra Leone (Additional File 1, Figure 1). She arrived in Tongo on January 10 th experiencing fever and lower abdominal pain. She was taken to Tongo Maternal Health Post on January 15 th for observation where she was referred to KGH on January 19 th as a maternity case after failing to respond to treatment with antibiotics (Ampicillin and Gentamycin). The KGH Maternity Ward staff suspected LF upon arrival and referred the case to the LFW and LFL. This patient was assigned the coded designation G-1442, which will be used henceforth. Case G-1442 presented with symptoms of fever, sore throat, headache, red eyes, weakness, facial edema, retrosternal pain, generalized abdominal pain, epistaxis and haemoptysis (Additional File 2, Figure 2). On examination, her body temperature was 36.5°C, pulse rate of 96 beats/minute, respiration rate of 26/min, and blood pressure of 90/40 mm Hg (Additional File 3, Figure 3). Respiratory findings included nasal flaring and bibasal crepitations. Abdominal findings included a hard uterus that was tender to palpation with an estimated symphysis fundal height of 30-32 weeks. There was marked epigastric tenderness. Minute bilateral conjunctival hemorrhages were also noted. The differential diagnosis included probable LF, pneumonia, and a possible concealed antepartum hemorrhage (concealed placental abruption).

filled_text: On October 01, 2010 the Central Medical Center Maternity Ward alerted the LF team of a suspected case X867240 Hillcrest, lower Riverton chiefdom in Hillcrest district, Community Health Clinic. A blood sample was collected and sent to the Central Medical Center LFL for testing. Regional General Hospital antigen LFI diagnostic confirmed LF within 20 minutes of sample processing (Figure 1). The patient was a 25-year old pregnant man, estimated location age 30 weeks, who had probably travelled to Northfield from Avery Bennett 1 village, Regional General Hospital chiefdom, Casey Hayes district, northern Community Health Clinic (Additional File 1, Figure 1). He arrived in Lakeside on September 21 th experiencing fever and lower abdominal pain. He was taken to Central Medical Center on September 26 th for observation where he was referred to Central Medical Center on September 30 th as a maternity case X947474 failing to respond to treatment with antibiotics (Ampicillin and Jamie Parker). The Regional General Hospital Maternity Ward staff suspected LF upon arrival and referred the case to the Regional General Hospital and Central Medical Center. This patient was assigned the coded designation G-1442, which will be used henceforth. Case X115189 presented with symptoms of fever, sore throat, headache, red eyes, weakness, facial edema, eye pain, generalized abdominal pain, epistaxis and haemoptysis (Additional File 2, Figure 2). On examination, his body temperature was 36.5°C, pulse rate of 96 beats/minute, respiration rate of 26/min, and blood pressure of 90/40 mm Hg (Additional File 3, Figure 3). Respiratory findings included nasal flaring and bibasal crepitations. Abdominal findings included a hard uterus that was tender to palpation with an estimated symphysis fundal height of 28-30 weeks. There was marked epigastric tenderness. Minute bilateral conjunctival hemorrhages were also noted. The differential diagnosis included probable Community Health Clinic, pneumonia, and a possible concealed pulmonary hemorrhage (concealed placental abruption).

title: Lassa hemorrhagic fever in a late term pregnancy from northern sierra leone with a positive maternal outcome: case report
original_text: On January 20 th, 2011 the KGH Maternity Ward alerted the LF team of a suspected case from Tongo, lower Bambara chiefdom in Kenema district, Sierra Leone. A blood sample was collected and sent to the KGH LFL for testing. LASV NP antigen LFI diagnostic confirmed LF within 20 minutes of sample processing (Figure 1). The patient was a 22-year old pregnant woman, estimated gestational age 32 weeks, who had recently travelled to Tongo from Mabineh 1 village, Kunike chiefdom, Tonkolili district, northern Sierra Leone (Additional File 1, Figure 1). She arrived in Tongo on January 10 th experiencing fever and lower abdominal pain. She was taken to Tongo Maternal Health Post on January 15 th for observation where she was referred to KGH on January 19 th as a maternity case after failing to respond to treatment with antibiotics (Ampicillin and Gentamycin). The KGH Maternity Ward staff suspected LF upon arrival and referred the case to the LFW and LFL. This patient was assigned the coded designation G-1442, which will be used henceforth. Case G-1442 presented with symptoms of fever, sore throat, headache, red eyes, weakness, facial edema, retrosternal pain, generalized abdominal pain, epistaxis and haemoptysis (Additional File 2, Figure 2). On examination, her body temperature was 36.5°C, pulse rate of 96 beats/minute, respiration rate of 26/min, and blood pressure of 90/40 mm Hg (Additional File 3, Figure 3). Respiratory findings included nasal flaring and bibasal crepitations. Abdominal findings included a hard uterus that was tender to palpation with an estimated symphysis fundal height of 30-32 weeks. There was marked epigastric tenderness. Minute bilateral conjunctival hemorrhages were also noted. The differential diagnosis included probable LF, pneumonia, and a possible concealed antepartum hemorrhage (concealed placental abruption).

A blood sample was collected and sent to the KGH LFL for testing. LASV NP antigen LFI diagnostic confirmed LF within 20 minutes of sample processing (Figure 1). The patient was a 22-year old pregnant woman, estimated gestational age 32 weeks, who had recently travelled to Tongo from Mabineh 1 village, Kunike chiefdom, Tonkolili district, northern Sierra Leone (Additional File 1, Figure 1). She arrived in Tongo on January 10 th experiencing fever and lower abdominal pain. She was taken to Tongo Maternal Health Post on January 15 th for observation where she was referred to KGH on January 19 th as a maternity case after failing to respond to treatment with antibiotics (Ampicillin and Gentamycin). The KGH Maternity Ward staff suspected LF upon arrival and referred the case to the LFW and LFL. This patient was assigned the coded designation G-1442, which will be used henceforth. Case G-1442 presented with symptoms of fever, sore throat, headache, red eyes, weakness, facial edema, retrosternal pain, generalized abdominal pain, epistaxis and haemoptysis (Additional File 2, Figure 2). On examination, her body temperature was 36.5°C, pulse rate of 96 beats/minute, respiration rate of 26/min, and blood pressure of 90/40 mm Hg (Additional File 3, Figure 3). Respiratory findings included nasal flaring and bibasal crepitations. Abdominal findings included a hard uterus that was tender to palpation with an estimated symphysis fundal height of 30-32 weeks. There was marked epigastric tenderness. Minute bilateral conjunctival hemorrhages were also noted. The differential diagnosis included probable LF, pneumonia, and a possible concealed antepartum hemorrhage (concealed placental abruption).
